title: HTML & CSS Academy
tagline: From your first tag to a real, responsive website
summary: Learn to build real websites from zero — visually. Every lesson pairs plain-language theory with a live code playground and interactive visualizers, so you see exactly what your code does. Free forever, beginner-friendly, bilingual, and built to take you all the way from your first <h1> to a responsive, professional layout.

modules.title: How the Web Works
modules.summary: Browsers, servers, domains, hosting and DNS — the journey of a web page, explained with simple visuals.
modules.outcome: You can explain what happens between typing a web address and seeing a page, and define browser, server, domain, hosting and DNS in plain words.
modules.intro: Before you build for the web, it helps to know — in plain language — what actually happens when you visit a site. You don't need anything technical here; just a clear picture. Once you have it, words like 'server', 'domain' and 'hosting' stop being mysterious, and everything you build afterwards makes more sense.

topics.title: The journey of a web page
topics.html:
When you type vidaara.org and press Enter, a quick conversation happens behind the scenes:

  1. Your browser asks DNS (the web's phone book) what numeric address belongs to vidaara.org.
  2. DNS replies with the IP address of the server.
  3. The browser asks that server for the page.
  4. The server sends back the HTML, CSS and images, and the browser assembles them into the page you see.
All of this usually happens in well under a second, every single time you open a page.
keyPoints: Visiting a site is a conversation: browser → DNS → server → page.
DNS turns a human address (vidaara.org) into a numeric IP address.
The server sends back HTML, CSS and images; the browser assembles them.

topics.title: The words, in plain language
topics.html:
WordIn plain English
BrowserThe app you view websites in — Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge. It requests pages and draws them.
ServerA computer, always on, that stores a website and sends it out when asked. "The site is hosted on a server."
DomainThe human-friendly address you type, like vidaara.org. You rent one from a registrar.
HostingRenting space on a server to keep your website's files. Your domain points to your hosting.
DNSThe Domain Name System — the web's phone book, matching domains to server IP addresses.
A simple way to hold it: a domain is like your home address, hosting is the actual house where your stuff lives, and DNS is the directory that tells the postman which house your address points to.

Here's the encouraging part: the websites you're about to build are just HTML and CSS files. Put them on hosting, point a domain at them, and the whole journey above carries them to anyone in the world. You already understand the destination — now you'll learn to build what arrives.
keyPoints: Browser = the app that views sites; Server = the always-on computer that stores and sends them.
Domain = the address you type; Hosting = the space on a server holding your files.
DNS = the phone book matching domains to server addresses.
A website is just HTML/CSS files on hosting, reached via a domain.

practical.title: Practical: trace the journey
practical.intro: No code this time — just check your understanding by explaining each step in your own words:
steps: In one sentence, what does the browser ask DNS for?
What does the server send back to the browser?
Explain the difference between a domain and hosting.
Name the browser you're using right now and one other.

questions.text: What is the job of DNS?
options: To match a domain name to a server's numeric IP address
To draw the page on screen
questions.explanation: DNS is the web's phone book — it translates a human address like vidaara.org into the server's IP address.

questions.text: What is a server?
options: An always-on computer that stores a website and sends it when asked
questions.explanation: A server is a computer that hosts a website's files and serves them to browsers on request.

questions.text: What is a domain?
options: The human-friendly address you type, like vidaara.org
questions.explanation: A domain is the readable address (vidaara.org) that points, via DNS, to a server.

questions.text: What does 'hosting' mean?
options: Renting space on a server to store your website's files
questions.explanation: Hosting is space on a server where your site's files live; your domain points to it.

questions.text: Which app draws the web page for you to see?
questions.explanation: The browser (Chrome, Firefox, etc.) requests the files and assembles them into the page you view.

modules.title: Introduction to HTML
modules.summary: What HTML is, the skeleton that sits behind every web page, and your very first live edit.
modules.outcome: You can explain what HTML is, recognise the basic structure of a web page, and write and change real HTML in a live editor.
modules.intro: Every website you have ever visited — Google, YouTube, your bank, this page — is built on HTML. It is the very first thing to learn, and the good news is that it is genuinely friendly. In this lesson we will not just read about HTML; you will write it and watch it come alive in the editor on this page. Let's get you to your first working web page in under a minute.

topics.title: What is HTML?
topics.html:
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. That sounds technical, but the idea is simple: HTML is how we describe the structure of a page to the browser. It is a set of labels — called tags — that you wrap around your content to say what each piece is.

Think of building a house. HTML is the bricks and rooms — the walls, the doorways, the layout. It is the structure. Later, CSS is the paint and furniture (how it looks) and JavaScript is the electricity (what it does). You always build the structure first.

Markup, not programming. HTML does not make decisions or do maths — it simply labels content. That is exactly why it is the perfect, gentle place to begin. There is nothing to be afraid of.

When you write a tag like <h1>, you are telling the browser: "this is the most important heading on the page." The browser then knows to show it big and bold, and a search engine knows it is the page's main title. One small label carries a lot of meaning.
keyPoints: HTML = HyperText Markup Language — it describes the structure of a page.
It uses tags to label content (this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is an image).
House analogy: HTML = bricks/structure, CSS = paint, JavaScript = electricity.
HTML is markup, not programming — there is no logic or maths to learn here.

topics.title: The skeleton of every web page
topics.html:
Almost every HTML page shares the same basic skeleton. You will type it so many times it will become second nature. Here is the structure, and what each part is for:

  • <!DOCTYPE html> — the very first line. It simply tells the browser "this is a modern HTML page."
  • <html> — the root. Everything else lives inside it.
  • <head> — information about the page that the visitor does not see directly: its title, character set, and links to styles. Think of it as the page's label and settings.
  • <body> — everything the visitor actually sees: headings, text, images, buttons.

Notice how tags nest inside one another, like boxes inside boxes. <title> sits inside <head>, which sits inside <html>. This nesting is what makes an HTML document a neat tree.

Read the playground below. It shows this exact skeleton. The code is on the left; the live web page it produces is on the right. Change the words inside <h1> and watch the preview update instantly.
keyPoints: Every page starts with <!DOCTYPE html>.
<html> is the root; inside it sit <head> (settings, not visible) and <body> (the visible content).
Tags nest inside one another like boxes in boxes, forming a tree.
Only what is inside <body> appears on the page; <title> appears on the browser tab.

topics.title: Your first edit — ship something now
topics.html:
Enough reading — let's make something that is yours. The playground below starts with a tiny page. Replace Your name here with your actual name and watch the preview change. That is it. You just edited a real web page.

Then try a few things, one at a time:

  • Change the heading text and the paragraph text.
  • Add a second paragraph by writing another <p>...</p> line under the first.
  • Try wrapping a word in <strong> and </strong> to make it bold — for example <strong>hello</strong>.
You cannot break anything. This editor is a safe sandbox that runs only on your screen. Experiment freely — if it ever looks wrong, press Reset and you are back to the start.
keyPoints: You edit HTML on the left and see the real web page on the right, live.
Add a paragraph with <p>...</p>; make text bold with <strong>...</strong>.
The playground is a safe sandbox — you cannot break anything, and Reset restores the start.

practical.title: Practical: a one-line bio page
practical.intro: Use the playground in topic 3 to build a tiny page about yourself. Aim for:
steps: An <h1> heading with your name.
One <p> paragraph saying where you are from and one thing you like.
A second <p> paragraph naming one thing you want to learn to build.
Make at least one word bold using <strong>.

questions.text: What does HTML stand for?
questions.explanation: HTML = HyperText Markup Language. It is a markup language that labels the structure of a page.

questions.text: Which part of the page holds the content the visitor actually sees?
questions.explanation: Everything visible on the page lives inside <body>. The <head> holds settings and the title, which is not shown on the page itself.

questions.text: In the house analogy used in this lesson, HTML is the…
questions.explanation: HTML is the bricks and structure. CSS is the paint/furniture (looks) and JavaScript is the electricity (behaviour).

questions.text: Where does the text inside <title> appear?
options: As the biggest heading on the page
At the bottom of the page
questions.explanation: The <title> (inside <head>) shows on the browser tab and in search results — not as content on the page.

questions.text: Which statement about HTML is true?
options: It does maths and makes decisions
It is a markup language that labels content
It controls the colours and fonts of a page
It only works on mobile phones
questions.explanation: HTML is markup — it labels content's structure. Colours and fonts are CSS's job; logic and maths are JavaScript's.

modules.title: Elements & Tags
modules.summary: The anatomy of an HTML element — opening tags, closing tags, void elements, and how nesting builds a tree.
modules.outcome: You can name the parts of an element, spot which tags need closing, and nest elements correctly without breaking the structure.
modules.intro: In the last lesson you met the page skeleton. Now we zoom right in on the building block it is made of: the element. Once you can read an element the way you read a word, the rest of HTML is just vocabulary.

topics.title: The anatomy of an element
topics.html:
Most HTML elements are written as a pair of tags wrapped around some content:

  • The opening tag — <p> — marks where the element starts.
  • The content — the text or other elements inside.
  • The closing tag — </p> — marks where it ends. Note the forward slash; that slash is the only difference, and forgetting it is the single most common beginner mistake.
Read it out loud: "paragraph, Hello, end paragraph." The closing tag always repeats the name with a / in front.
keyPoints: An element is usually an opening tag + content + closing tag.
The closing tag repeats the name with a slash: <p> … </p>.
Forgetting the closing slash is the most common beginner error.

topics.title: Void elements — tags that stand alone
topics.html:
A few elements have no content, so they have no closing tag. These are called void (or empty) elements. They do their job in a single tag:

  • <br> — a line break.
  • <hr> — a horizontal divider line.
  • <img> — an image (you give it a source instead of content).
  • <input> — a form field.
You may sometimes see them written with a trailing slash like <br />. In modern HTML that slash is optional and does nothing — <br> is perfectly correct.
keyPoints: Void elements like <br>, <hr>, <img> and <input> have no content and no closing tag.
The trailing slash in <br /> is optional in modern HTML.

topics.title: Nesting — elements inside elements
topics.html:
Elements live inside other elements, forming a tree of parents and children. The golden rule: tags must close in the reverse order they opened, like closing a set of brackets.

Correct — the inner element closes first:

<p>This is <strong>very</strong> important.</p>

Wrong — the tags overlap and cross over:

<p>This is <strong>very</p></strong>

Try it yourself below. The editor keeps a <strong> word inside a paragraph — add an <em> (italic) word too, making sure every tag you open, you close.
keyPoints: Elements nest to form a tree of parents and children.
Tags must close in reverse order — the inner tag closes before the outer one.
Overlapping tags like <strong>…</p></strong> are invalid.

practical.title: Practical: a tiny nested page
practical.intro: In the playground above, build three lines:
steps: A paragraph with one <strong> (bold) word.
A paragraph with one <em> (italic) word.
A single <hr> between them — and notice it needs no closing tag.
Confirm every opening tag has a matching closing tag (except the void <hr>).

questions.text: What is the closing tag for <p>?
questions.explanation: A closing tag repeats the element name with a forward slash in front: </p>.

questions.text: Which of these is a void (empty) element with no closing tag?
questions.explanation: <img> is a void element — it has no content and therefore no closing tag. So are <br>, <hr> and <input>.

questions.text: Which line is correctly nested?
questions.explanation: The inner element must close before the outer one: open p, open strong, close strong, close p.

questions.text: What is the single most common beginner mistake when writing tags?
questions.explanation: Forgetting to close a tag (the /) is the classic mistake — it leaves the element open and can break the rest of the page.

questions.text: In <p>This is <em>great</em></p>, what is the <em> element?
questions.explanation: The <em> element sits inside the paragraph, so it is a child of the <p> parent.

modules.title: Attributes
modules.summary: Give elements extra information — id, class, href, src, alt and more — written the right way on the opening tag.
modules.outcome: You can add attributes correctly, know the difference between id and class, and recognise the everyday attributes you will use on almost every page.
modules.intro: Tags tell the browser what an element is. Attributes tell it more about that element — where a link goes, which image to show, what a section is called. They are how you turn a plain tag into something useful.

topics.title: How an attribute is written
topics.html:
Attributes always go inside the opening tag, after the tag name, written as name="value":

  • The name says which attribute it is (here, href — the link's destination).
  • The value goes in quotes after an equals sign.
  • You can add several attributes, separated by spaces: <img src="cat.jpg" alt="A cat">.
Always wrap values in quotes. <a href=/about> may sometimes work, but a value with a space — like a title — will break without quotes. Quote everything and you will never get caught out.
keyPoints: Attributes go inside the opening tag as name="value".
Separate multiple attributes with spaces.
Always wrap the value in quotes — it avoids a whole class of bugs.

topics.title: The attributes you'll use most
topics.html:
AttributeUsed onWhat it does
href<a>The address a link points to.
src<img>, mediaThe file source to load.
alt<img>Text description of an image (vital for accessibility and SEO).
idany elementA unique name for one element on the page.
classany elementA shared label you can reuse on many elements (mainly for CSS).

id vs class — the one thing to remember

An id must be unique — only one element on the whole page may have a given id, like a passport number. A class can be reused on as many elements as you like, like a job title. You will lean on class constantly once you reach CSS.
keyPoints: href sets a link's destination; src sets a file to load; alt describes an image.
id is unique (one per page); class is reusable across many elements.
You will use class heavily once you start writing CSS.

practical.title: Practical: a described image link
practical.intro: Using what you know, write (in any playground):
steps: An <a> element with an href pointing to a website you like.
Add a title attribute so a tooltip appears on hover.
Give the link a class="cta" so you could style it later.
Confirm every attribute value is wrapped in quotes.

questions.text: Where do attributes go?
questions.explanation: Attributes are written inside the opening tag, after the tag name, as name="value".

questions.text: Which attribute gives an image its text description?
questions.explanation: alt provides alternative text — read by screen readers and search engines, and shown if the image fails to load.

questions.text: What is the key difference between id and class?
options: id is for CSS, class is for JavaScript
id must be unique on the page; class can be reused
class must be unique; id can be reused
questions.explanation: An id must be unique to one element on the page; a class can be shared by many elements.

questions.text: Which attribute sets where a link points?
questions.explanation: href (hypertext reference) on an <a> element sets the link's destination.

questions.text: Why should attribute values always be wrapped in quotes?
options: It makes the page load faster
Values containing spaces break without quotes
It changes the colour of the text
questions.explanation: Unquoted values can work for simple cases, but any value with a space breaks. Quoting everything avoids the whole problem.

modules.title: Headings & Paragraphs
modules.summary: Structure your text with h1–h6 and paragraphs, and learn why heading order matters for SEO and accessibility.
modules.outcome: You can structure a page with a correct heading hierarchy, write paragraphs properly, and avoid the common 'using headings just to make text big' trap.
modules.intro: Text is the heart of the web, and HTML gives it shape with two everyday elements: headings and paragraphs. Used well, they make a page easy to scan for people and for search engines. Used carelessly, they quietly hurt both.

topics.title: Six levels of heading
topics.html:
HTML has six heading levels, from <h1> (most important) down to <h6> (least). Think of them like a document outline:

<h1>Cooking at Home</h1>        (the page title — only one)
  <h2>Breakfast</h2>            (a major section)
    <h3>Quick eggs</h3>        (a sub-topic)
  <h2>Lunch</h2>
One rule above all: use exactly one <h1> per page — it is the page's main title — and never skip levels (don't jump from <h2> straight to <h4>). Screen readers let users jump between headings, so a clean order is a real kindness.
Do not pick a heading just because it looks big. If you want big text, that is a job for CSS later. Headings are about meaning and structure, not size.
keyPoints: Headings run from <h1> (most important) to <h6> (least).
Use exactly one <h1> per page and never skip levels.
Choose a heading for its meaning, not its size — size is CSS's job.

topics.title: Paragraphs and line breaks
topics.html:
Body text goes in <p> (paragraph) elements. Each paragraph is a separate block with space around it. Pressing Enter in your code does not create a new paragraph — you must wrap each one in its own <p> tags.

For a soft line break within a paragraph — like lines of an address or a poem — use the void element <br>. But do not use a pile of <br> tags to fake spacing between paragraphs; that is what separate <p> elements are for.
keyPoints: Each paragraph needs its own <p> tags — pressing Enter in code does nothing.
<br> makes a soft line break inside a paragraph.
Don't stack <br> tags to space things out — use separate paragraphs.

practical.title: Practical: a structured mini-article
practical.intro: Build a small article in any playground:
steps: One <h1> with the article's title.
Two <h2> sections, each followed by a <p> paragraph.
Inside one paragraph, use a <br> for a single line break.
Check you used exactly one <h1> and did not skip from h1 to h3.

questions.text: How many <h1> elements should a page normally have?
questions.explanation: A page should have exactly one <h1> — its main title. Other sections use <h2> and below.

questions.text: You want a big, bold line of text. What is the correct approach?
options: Use an <h1> because it looks big
Choose the heading by meaning, and make text big with CSS later
questions.explanation: Headings describe structure, not size. Pick the right level for meaning, and use CSS to control appearance.

questions.text: Which is bad practice when ordering headings?
questions.explanation: Skipping levels breaks the outline and confuses screen-reader users who navigate by heading.

questions.text: Pressing Enter in your HTML code to separate two blocks of text will…
options: Do nothing visible — you must wrap each in <p>
questions.explanation: Whitespace in code is collapsed. To get separate paragraphs you must wrap each in its own <p> element.

questions.text: Which element gives a single line break inside a paragraph?
questions.explanation: <br> is a void element that inserts a single line break within a block of text.

modules.title: Lists
modules.summary: Ordered, unordered, nested and description lists — the backbone of menus, steps and structured content.
modules.outcome: You can build bullet and numbered lists, nest them, and choose the right list type for the job — including for navigation menus.
modules.intro: Lists are everywhere on the web: navigation menus, recipe steps, feature bullets, FAQs. HTML gives you three kinds, and picking the right one keeps your markup meaningful.

topics.title: Unordered and ordered lists
topics.html:
Both list types are built the same way: a container element holding list items (<li>). Only the container changes.

ListContainerUse when…
Unordered<ul>order does not matter (a shopping list, features). Shows bullets.
Ordered<ol>order matters (steps, rankings). Shows numbers.
<ul>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Bread</li>
</ul>
Only <li> elements belong directly inside a <ul> or <ol> — not loose text or paragraphs.
keyPoints: Use <ul> for unordered (bulleted) lists and <ol> for ordered (numbered) lists.
Both hold <li> (list item) elements.
Only <li> belongs directly inside a list — not loose text.

topics.title: Nested lists, and lists as menus
topics.html:
A list item can contain another whole list, giving you sub-points:

<ul>
  <li>Fruit
    <ul>
      <li>Apple</li>
      <li>Mango</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

Here's something that surprises beginners: almost every website's navigation menu is really an unordered list of links. It is the semantically correct structure — a list of places you can go. You will see this pattern constantly:

<nav>
  <ul>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>
There is also a third type — the description list (<dl> with <dt> terms and <dd> definitions) — handy for glossaries and FAQs.
keyPoints: Nest a list by placing a <ul> or <ol> inside an <li>.
Navigation menus are correctly built as a <ul> of links inside <nav>.
Description lists (<dl>/<dt>/<dd>) suit glossaries and FAQs.

practical.title: Practical: a menu and a recipe
practical.intro: In any playground, create:
steps: An ordered list (<ol>) of 3 steps to make tea.
An unordered list (<ul>) of 3 ingredients.
A nested list — one ingredient with two sub-items under it.
Bonus: a <ul> of links wrapped in a <nav> as a menu.

questions.text: Which list type shows numbers and is for steps where order matters?
questions.explanation: <ol> is the ordered list — the browser numbers the items automatically.

questions.text: What element holds each item inside a <ul> or <ol>?
questions.explanation: List items are wrapped in <li> elements.

questions.text: How do you create a sub-list under an item?
options: Add a second <ul> after the list
questions.explanation: Nest by placing another list inside the <li> you want to expand.

questions.text: What is the semantically correct structure for a navigation menu?
questions.explanation: A menu is a list of places to go, so a <ul> of <a> links inside <nav> is the right structure.

questions.text: Which list type best suits a glossary of terms and their definitions?
questions.explanation: A description list pairs each <dt> term with its <dd> definition — ideal for glossaries and FAQs.

modules.title: Links
modules.summary: Connect pages with the anchor element — internal and external links, anchor jumps, and safe new-tab links.
modules.outcome: You can create links to other pages and sites, jump to a section on the same page, and open links in a new tab safely.
modules.intro: The 'HT' in HTML stands for HyperText — and links are what make it 'hyper'. A link, or anchor, is what turns a pile of pages into a connected web. It is one of the most important elements you will ever write.

topics.title: The anchor element
topics.html:
A link is an <a> element with an href attribute pointing to a destination. The text between the tags is what the user clicks:

<a href="https://vidaara.org">Visit Vidaara</a>

There are two kinds of destination:

  • Absolute — a full address starting with https://. Use it to link to other websites.
  • Relative — a path on your own site, like /about or contact.html. Use it to link between your own pages.
Write link text that makes sense on its own. "Read our refund policy" is far better than "click here" — search engines and screen-reader users rely on the link text to know where it leads.
keyPoints: A link is <a href="…">text</a>.
Absolute URLs (https://…) link to other sites; relative paths (/about) link within your own.
Write descriptive link text — never "click here".

topics.title: New tabs, jumps and email links
topics.html:
A few common variations you will reach for often:

Open in a new tab — safely

Add target="_blank" to open a link in a new tab. When you do, always add rel="noopener noreferrer" too — it closes a small security and performance hole:

<a href="https://example.com"
   target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">External site</a>

Jump to a section on the same page

If an element has an id, you can link to it with # plus that id — handy for a table of contents: <a href="#faq">Jump to FAQ</a> jumps to <section id="faq">.

Email and phone links

<a href="mailto:hi@vidaara.org">Email us</a> opens the visitor's email app; tel: works the same for phone numbers on mobiles.
keyPoints: target="_blank" opens a new tab — always pair it with rel="noopener noreferrer".
Link to a section with href="#id" matching an element's id.
mailto: and tel: links open the email or phone app.

practical.title: Practical: a tiny link hub
practical.intro: In any playground, create a short page with:
steps: A link to an external website (absolute URL) that opens in a new tab safely.
A relative link to a made-up page on your own site, e.g. /about.
An email link using mailto:.
Make sure each link's text describes where it goes.

questions.text: Which attribute holds a link's destination?
questions.explanation: The href attribute on an <a> element sets where the link points.

questions.text: You add target="_blank" to open a link in a new tab. What else should you add?
questions.explanation: rel="noopener noreferrer" closes a security and performance hole that target="_blank" can otherwise open.

questions.text: How do you link to a section with id="faq" on the same page?
questions.explanation: A # followed by the element's id jumps to that element on the current page.

questions.text: Which is the better link text?
questions.explanation: Descriptive text like "Read our refund policy" tells users and search engines where the link goes; "click here" tells them nothing.

questions.text: What does <a href="mailto:hi@vidaara.org"> do?
options: Opens the visitor's email app with the address filled in
Links to a page called mailto
questions.explanation: A mailto: link opens the visitor's default email app with the recipient pre-filled.

modules.title: Images
modules.summary: Add images that load fast, never break the layout, and always carry meaningful alt text.
modules.outcome: You can place an image with the right src and alt, understand why alt text matters, and keep images from overflowing or slowing the page.
modules.intro: A page without images feels bare — but images done badly are also the number-one cause of slow, broken-looking websites. The <img> element is simple, and getting two attributes right (src and alt) puts you ahead of a surprising number of real sites.

topics.title: The img element
topics.html:
<img> is a void element — no closing tag. Instead of content, you point it at a file with src and describe it with alt:

<img src="logo.png" alt="Vidaara logo">
  • src — the image file. It can be a relative path (images/logo.png), an absolute URL, or a data URI.
  • alt — a short text description. This is not optional in practice: screen readers read it aloud, search engines index it, and it shows if the image fails to load.
Never leave out alt on a content image. Write what the image shows ("Students planting trees"), not "image of…". For purely decorative images, use an empty alt="" so screen readers skip them.
keyPoints: <img> is a void element — no closing tag.
src points to the image file; alt describes it.
Always write meaningful alt for content images; use alt="" for purely decorative ones.

topics.title: Fast, responsive images
topics.html:
Two habits keep images from hurting your page:

Don't let images overflow

A big image can blow out your layout on a phone. The standard fix (you'll meet it again in the CSS track) is one CSS rule: img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }. This lets an image shrink to fit its container while keeping its proportions.

Help the browser and save data

  • Add width and height attributes so the browser reserves space and the page doesn't jump around as images load.
  • Add loading="lazy" so off-screen images only download when the user scrolls near them — a real saving on slow connections.
  • Choose a sensibly sized file. A 4000-pixel photo for a small thumbnail wastes your visitor's data, especially on mobile.
<img src="team.jpg" alt="Our volunteers"
     width="800" height="500" loading="lazy">
keyPoints: img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } stops images overflowing on small screens.
Set width and height so the page doesn't jump as images load.
loading="lazy" defers off-screen images, saving data on slow connections.

practical.title: Practical: a captioned, accessible image
practical.intro: In any playground, add an image with:
steps: An <img> with a meaningful alt describing what it shows.
A <p> caption underneath it.
Add loading="lazy" to the image.
Empty the src value once to confirm the alt text appears in its place.

questions.text: Which attribute provides a text description of an image?
questions.explanation: alt describes the image for screen readers, search engines, and as a fallback when the image fails to load.

questions.text: Is <img> a void element?
options: Yes — it has no closing tag
Only when it has alt text
questions.explanation: <img> is void: it takes its source from src and needs no closing tag.

questions.text: For a purely decorative image, what should alt be?
questions.explanation: An empty alt="" tells screen readers to skip a decorative image, while still being valid HTML.

questions.text: Which CSS rule keeps an image from overflowing its container?
questions.explanation: max-width: 100% lets the image shrink to fit, and height: auto keeps its proportions.

questions.text: What does loading="lazy" do?
options: Loads off-screen images only when the user scrolls near them
Makes the image load faster always
questions.explanation: Lazy loading defers images that are not yet visible, saving bandwidth — a real benefit on slow connections.

modules.title: Tables
modules.summary: Rows, columns, headers and captions — build accessible data tables the right way, and know when not to use them.
modules.outcome: You can build a table with proper header cells and a caption, and you understand that tables are for data, not page layout.
modules.intro: Tables show up wherever data lines up in rows and columns: price lists, timetables, scoreboards. They have a few moving parts, but the structure is logical once you see it. We'll also clear up the most important myth about tables.

topics.title: The parts of a table
topics.html:
A table is built from a handful of nested elements:

ElementRole
<table>The whole table.
<tr>A table row.
<th>A header cell (bold, and announced as a header by screen readers).
<td>A normal data cell.
<caption>A title for the table — the first child of <table>.

Group rows with <thead> (header rows) and <tbody> (the data) for clarity and styling.

<table>
  <caption>Class timetable</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Day</th><th>Subject</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Mon</td><td>Maths</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
keyPoints: <table> holds rows (<tr>); rows hold header cells (<th>) and data cells (<td>).
<caption> titles the table and should be its first child.
Group rows with <thead> and <tbody>.

topics.title: Accessible tables — and the layout myth
topics.html:
Use <th> for header cells, not styled <td>. Screen readers use them to announce "Day: Monday, Subject: Maths" instead of reading a wall of disconnected values. For complex tables, add scope="col" or scope="row" to say which way a header applies.

The big myth: years ago people built entire page layouts with tables. Do not do this. Tables are for tabular data only. For page layout — sidebars, columns, grids — you use CSS Flexbox and Grid (coming up in the CSS track). Using a table for layout breaks screen readers and makes pages rigid on mobile.

On small screens, wrap a wide table in a container with overflow-x: auto so it can scroll sideways instead of breaking the page.
keyPoints: Use <th> for real header cells so screen readers can pair headers with data.
Add scope="col" / scope="row" on headers in complex tables.
Never use tables for page layout — that's a job for CSS Flexbox/Grid.

practical.title: Practical: a price list
practical.intro: In any playground, build a table with:
steps: A <caption> titling the table.
A header row of <th> cells inside <thead>.
At least three data rows inside <tbody>.
Confirm you used <th> for headers, not bold <td>.

questions.text: Which element is a table header cell?
questions.explanation: <th> is a header cell — bold by default and announced as a header by screen readers.

questions.text: What does <tr> represent?
questions.explanation: <tr> is a table row, containing <th> and/or <td> cells.

questions.text: Where should <caption> go?
questions.explanation: The <caption> is the table's title and belongs as its first child.

questions.text: Should you use a table to lay out the columns of your page?
options: Yes, that's what tables are for
No — use CSS Flexbox or Grid; tables are for data
Only if you add a caption
questions.explanation: Tables are for tabular data. Page layout is done with CSS Flexbox/Grid; table layouts break accessibility and mobile.

questions.text: How do you stop a wide table from breaking the layout on mobile?
options: Wrap it in a container with overflow-x: auto
questions.explanation: Wrapping the table in a scrollable container (overflow-x: auto) lets it scroll sideways instead of overflowing the page.

modules.title: Forms
modules.summary: Inputs, labels, buttons and validation — how to collect information from your visitors, accessibly.
modules.outcome: You can build a form with properly labelled inputs of different types, mark fields required, and explain why every input needs a label.
modules.intro: Forms are how the web listens: sign-ups, searches, contact pages, checkouts. The HTML side is very approachable, and getting one detail right — pairing every input with a label — instantly makes your forms more usable and accessible than most you'll meet online.

topics.title: Inputs and their labels
topics.html:
A form lives in a <form> element. Inside it, the workhorse is <input>, a void element whose type attribute changes what it collects:

typeGives you
textA single line of text.
emailA text box that checks for an @ and shows an email keyboard on phones.
passwordHidden, dotted-out text.
numberA numeric field with up/down arrows.
checkbox / radioTick boxes / pick-one options.

Always label your inputs

Every input needs a <label>. Link them by giving the input an id and the label a matching for:

<label for="email">Your email</label>
<input type="email" id="email">
A linked label isn't just neat — clicking it focuses the input (a bigger tap target on mobile), and screen readers announce the field's purpose. Never ship an input without one.
keyPoints: Inputs live in a <form>; the type attribute decides what each <input> collects.
Pair every input with a <label> using matching for and id.
A linked label improves accessibility and gives a bigger tap target on mobile.

topics.title: More controls and basic validation
topics.html:
Beyond <input>, you'll reach for:

  • <textarea> — a multi-line text box (e.g. a message).
  • <select> with <option>s — a dropdown menu.
  • <button> — typically type="submit" to send the form.

Built-in validation

The browser can check fields for you before sending, with simple attributes:

  • required — the field must be filled in.
  • minlength / maxlength — limit text length.
  • type="email" — must look like an email.
Important: browser validation is a convenience, not security. A determined user can bypass it. Always validate again on the server (your Node/Laravel back-end) — never trust the browser alone.
keyPoints: Use <textarea> for long text, <select> for dropdowns, <button type="submit"> to send.
Attributes like required, minlength and type="email" give free browser validation.
Browser validation is convenience only — always validate on the server too.

practical.title: Practical: a contact form
practical.intro: In any playground, build a small contact form with:
steps: A labelled text input for a name, marked required.
A labelled email input.
A labelled <textarea> for a message.
A <button type="submit">, and confirm every field has a matching label.

questions.text: How do you link a <label> to its input?
options: Put the input's text inside the label's id
Give the input an id and the label a matching for
questions.explanation: The label's for must match the input's id — that connects them for clicks and screen readers.

questions.text: Which input type shows dotted-out, hidden text?
questions.explanation: type="password" masks the characters as the user types.

questions.text: Which attribute makes a field mandatory?
questions.explanation: Adding required tells the browser the field must be filled before the form can submit.

questions.text: Which element gives a multi-line text box?
questions.explanation: <textarea> provides a resizable multi-line text box.

questions.text: Is browser validation enough to keep your data safe?
options: Yes, it blocks all bad input
No — always validate on the server as well
questions.explanation: Browser validation can be bypassed, so it's a convenience only. The server must validate every submission too.

modules.title: Semantic HTML
modules.summary: header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer — write markup that means something, and score 100% on clean code.
modules.outcome: You can replace generic divs with the right semantic elements, and you understand why meaningful markup helps SEO, accessibility and your own sanity.
modules.intro: You can build a whole site with nothing but <div>. It will even look fine. But it's like writing a book with no chapter titles — technically readable, but nobody (and no search engine, and no screen reader) can tell what's what. Semantic HTML fixes that by giving each region a name that describes its purpose.

topics.title: div soup vs semantic structure
topics.html:
A <div> is a generic box with no meaning. "Div soup" is a page built entirely from them. Semantic elements replace the common ones with named regions:

Instead of…UseFor
<div><header>The top banner / intro of a page or section.
<div><nav>The main navigation links.
<div><main>The one main content area (one per page).
<div><article>A self-contained piece — a blog post, a card.
<div><section>A thematic grouping with its own heading.
<div><aside>Side content — related links, a sidebar.
<div><footer>The bottom — copyright, links.
<div> and <span> are still useful — reach for them when no semantic element fits and you just need a box (<div>) or an inline wrapper (<span>), usually for styling.
keyPoints: <div> is a box with no meaning; semantic elements name a region's purpose.
Common ones: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <footer>.
Use one <main> per page; fall back to <div>/<span> only when nothing semantic fits.

topics.title: Why it's worth it — your Semantic Score
topics.html:
Imagine a meter that scores how meaningful your markup is. A layout built from only <div> tags scores low; swap in the right semantic elements and it climbs toward 100%. That score is a stand-in for three real-world wins:

  • Accessibility — screen-reader users can jump straight to "main", "navigation" or "footer". Div soup gives them nothing to navigate by.
  • SEO — search engines understand your page structure better, which helps them surface the right content.
  • Maintainability — six months later, <article> and <aside> tell you what each block is at a glance; forty nested <div>s do not.
A quick self-test: read your tags aloud, ignoring the content. If you can describe the page's structure just from the element names, your Semantic Score is high.
keyPoints: Semantic markup boosts accessibility (landmark navigation), SEO and long-term maintainability.
A 'div-only' layout scores low; the right named elements push it toward 100%.
Self-test: if the tag names alone describe the page, your markup is semantic.

practical.title: Practical: convert div soup
practical.intro: In any playground, build a small page that uses real landmarks:
steps: A <header> containing an <h1> and a <nav>.
A <main> with one <article> inside.
An <aside> with a couple of related links.
A <footer> — and check you used no <div> where a semantic element fits.

questions.text: Which element is meant for the one main content area of a page?
questions.explanation: <main> wraps the primary content and should appear once per page.

questions.text: What is "div soup"?
options: A page built entirely from generic <div> elements with no semantic meaning
questions.explanation: Div soup is markup made only of meaningless <div>s — it works visually but conveys no structure.

questions.text: Which is a real benefit of semantic HTML?
options: It makes the page load instantly
Screen-reader users can navigate by landmarks like main and nav
It removes the need for CSS
It hides content from search engines
questions.explanation: Semantic landmarks let assistive tech jump to regions like navigation, main and footer — a major accessibility win.

questions.text: Which element best wraps a self-contained blog post?
questions.explanation: <article> is for a self-contained, independently distributable piece of content like a post.

questions.text: When is it fine to use a plain <div>?
options: When no semantic element fits and you need a box, usually for styling
questions.explanation: <div> (and <span>) are still valid as generic containers when no semantic element fits the purpose.

modules.title: Audio & Video
modules.summary: Embed sound and video natively with the audio and video elements — no plugins, with fallbacks and captions.
modules.outcome: You can add a working audio or video player with controls, provide multiple source formats, and include captions for accessibility.
modules.intro: It used to take clunky plugins to put media on a page. Today HTML does it natively with two elements: <audio> and <video>. They behave almost identically, so learn one and you know both.

topics.title: The video and audio elements
topics.html:
Give the element a src and the controls attribute to get a play/pause bar:

<video src="clip.mp4" controls width="480"></video>

<audio src="song.mp3" controls></audio>

Handy attributes (on both):

  • controls — show the play/pause/volume bar. Almost always include this.
  • poster (video only) — an image to show before play.
  • loop — repeat when finished.
  • muted — start silent.
Don't use autoplay with sound. It's jarring, eats mobile data, and browsers block it anyway. If you must autoplay (e.g. a background clip), it has to be muted.
keyPoints: <video> and <audio> embed media natively — no plugins.
Add controls to show the play/pause bar.
Never autoplay with sound; if you autoplay, it must be muted.

topics.title: Multiple sources, fallbacks and captions
topics.html:
Different browsers support different file formats. Instead of one src, you can offer several <source> elements and let the browser pick the first it can play. Put plain fallback text between the tags for very old browsers:

<video controls width="480">
  <source src="clip.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="clip.mp4"  type="video/mp4">
  Your browser can't play this video.
</video>

Captions = accessibility

Add a <track> with a captions file so deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers (and anyone watching with the sound off) can follow along:

<track kind="captions" src="clip.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">
Captions aren't optional polish — for a large audience they're the difference between usable and useless. They also help search engines understand your video.
keyPoints: Offer multiple <source> elements so the browser picks a format it supports.
Text between the tags is the fallback for browsers that can't play the media.
Add a <track kind="captions"> for captions — essential accessibility, not optional.

practical.title: Practical: a captioned video block
practical.intro: Write the markup (in any playground) for:
steps: A <video> with controls and a width.
Two <source> elements (webm and mp4).
A fallback line of text for unsupported browsers.
A <track kind="captions"> for an English captions file.

questions.text: Which attribute shows the play/pause/volume bar?
questions.explanation: Adding controls tells the browser to render its built-in media controls.

questions.text: Why offer multiple <source> elements?
options: To play several videos at once
So the browser can pick a file format it supports
questions.explanation: Browsers vary in which formats they support; multiple sources let each pick one it can play.

questions.text: What does the text between <video> and </video> do?
options: Is the fallback for browsers that can't play the video
questions.explanation: That text is fallback content shown only when the browser cannot play any of the sources.

questions.text: Which element adds captions to a video?
questions.explanation: <track kind="captions"> attaches a captions file (e.g. a .vtt) to the media.

questions.text: What's the rule about autoplay?
options: Never autoplay with sound; if you autoplay, it must be muted
questions.explanation: Autoplaying audio is jarring and browser-blocked. Any autoplay should be muted.

modules.title: Iframes
modules.summary: Embed another web page inside yours — maps, videos and widgets — safely and accessibly.
modules.outcome: You can embed external content with an iframe, give it a title for accessibility, and apply the sandbox and lazy-loading attributes to keep it safe and fast.
modules.intro: An <iframe> (inline frame) is a window in your page that shows another whole web page inside it. It's how you drop a YouTube video, a Google Map, or a payment widget into your site without rebuilding it. Powerful — and worth handling with a little care.

topics.title: Embedding a page
topics.html:
Point an iframe at a URL with src, and size it with width and height:

<iframe src="https://example.com"
        width="100%" height="300"
        title="Example site"></iframe>
Always add a title. Screen-reader users hear the title to know what the frame contains — without it they just hear "frame", which is useless. It's the most-skipped iframe accessibility step.

Most embeds (YouTube, Google Maps) give you a ready-made iframe snippet to copy. You usually only tweak its width, height and title.
keyPoints: <iframe src="…"> embeds another page as a window inside yours.
Size it with width and height.
Always add a title so screen-reader users know what the frame contains.

topics.title: Keep iframes safe and fast
topics.html:
Because an iframe runs someone else's page inside yours, two attributes matter:

  • loading="lazy" — don't load the frame until the user scrolls near it. Embeds are heavy; this is a big speed win, especially on mobile data.
  • sandbox — restrict what the embedded page can do (run scripts, submit forms, open pop-ups). You then opt back in only what's needed, e.g. sandbox="allow-scripts". An empty sandbox is the most locked-down.
Fun fact: the live playground you've been using on Vidaara is itself a sandboxed iframe — that's exactly why your code can run safely without affecting the rest of the page.

Only embed sources you trust, and prefer https:// URLs so the connection is encrypted.
keyPoints: loading="lazy" defers heavy embeds until needed — a real speed win.
sandbox restricts what the embedded page can do; opt back in only what's necessary.
Only embed trusted sources, and prefer https:// URLs.

practical.title: Practical: a safe embed
practical.intro: Write the markup (in any playground) for:
steps: An <iframe> with a src, a percentage width and a fixed height.
A descriptive title attribute.
Add loading="lazy" so it loads only when scrolled into view.
Add a sandbox attribute to lock it down.

questions.text: What does an <iframe> do?
options: Embeds another web page inside the current one
questions.explanation: An iframe is an inline frame — a window that displays another page inside yours.

questions.text: Why must you add a title to an iframe?
options: To show a heading above it
So screen-reader users know what the frame contains
questions.explanation: The title tells assistive tech what the embedded content is — without it, users just hear "frame".

questions.text: What does loading="lazy" do on an iframe?
options: Defers loading until the user scrolls near it
questions.explanation: Lazy loading delays the (often heavy) embed until it's about to be seen, saving bandwidth and speeding up the page.

questions.text: What is the sandbox attribute for?
options: Adding a play area for games
Restricting what the embedded page is allowed to do
questions.explanation: sandbox locks down the embedded page's capabilities (scripts, forms, pop-ups); you re-enable only what's needed.

questions.text: Which sources should you embed in an iframe?
options: Only sources you trust, ideally over https
questions.explanation: Because the embed runs inside your page's context, only embed trusted sources, preferably over an encrypted https connection.

modules.title: Accessibility (a11y)
modules.summary: Build pages everyone can use — including screen-reader and keyboard users — mostly by writing good HTML.
modules.outcome: You can make a page keyboard-usable, write meaningful alt text and labels, use native interactive elements, and apply ARIA only when you truly need it.
modules.intro: Accessibility (often shortened to a11y — 'a', then 11 letters, then 'y') means building so that people with disabilities can use your site: those who are blind, have low vision, can't use a mouse, or are hard of hearing. The wonderful part? Most of it is just good HTML, which you've already been learning. This lesson ties it together.

topics.title: Use the right element — it does the work for you
topics.html:
The single biggest accessibility win is using the correct native element. A real <button> is focusable with the keyboard, fires on Enter and Space, and is announced as "button" — all for free. A <div> styled to look like a button is none of those things; a keyboard user simply cannot reach it.

The same idea runs through everything you've learned:

  • <img alt="…"> — describe what the image shows.
  • <label for> — name every form field.
  • Semantic landmarks (<nav>, <main>) — let users jump around.
  • Heading order (one <h1>, no skipped levels) — gives a navigable outline.
Try the playground below with your keyboard: press Tab. The real button receives focus and works with Enter; the fake div button is skipped entirely.
keyPoints: Using the correct native element (e.g. <button>) gives keyboard support and screen-reader naming for free.
A <div> styled as a button can't be reached by keyboard users.
alt text, labels, semantic landmarks and heading order are all accessibility features you've already learned.

topics.title: Keyboard, focus and a little ARIA
topics.html:
Many people navigate entirely by keyboard. Two rules keep them happy:

  • Everything interactive must be reachable by Tab and operable by Enter/Space. Native elements handle this; custom widgets need extra care.
  • Never hide the focus outline. That glowing ring around the focused element shows keyboard users where they are. If a design removes it, you must add a clear replacement — removing it with outline: none and nothing else is an accessibility failure.

ARIA — the seasoning, not the meal

ARIA attributes (like aria-label or role) add accessibility information when HTML alone isn't enough — for example, aria-label="Close" on an icon-only button. But the first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA if a native element already does the job. Reaching for role="button" on a div is worse than just using a <button>.

Bad ARIA is worse than no ARIA — it can actively mislead screen readers. Use native HTML first; add ARIA only to fill a genuine gap.
keyPoints: Every interactive element must be reachable by <kbd>Tab</kbd> and work with Enter/Space.
Never remove the focus outline without providing a clear visible replacement.
Use ARIA only to fill gaps native HTML can't — prefer the right element over role hacks.

practical.title: Practical: a keyboard-friendly mini page
practical.intro: In any playground, build and then Tab through:
steps: A real <button> and confirm it receives focus on Tab.
An image with meaningful alt text.
A form field with a linked <label>.
Check every interactive thing is reachable by keyboard alone.

questions.text: What does "a11y" stand for?
questions.explanation: a11y is shorthand for accessibility — 'a', 11 letters, then 'y'.

questions.text: Why prefer a real <button> over a styled <div>?
options: It is keyboard-focusable and announced as a button for free
questions.explanation: A native button is reachable by Tab, works with Enter/Space, and is announced as a button — none of which a styled div provides.

questions.text: What is wrong with outline: none on focusable elements?
options: It removes the focus indicator keyboard users rely on
questions.explanation: The focus outline shows keyboard users where they are. Removing it without a clear replacement is an accessibility failure.

questions.text: What is the first rule of ARIA?
options: Don't use ARIA if a native element already does the job
questions.explanation: Native HTML elements have accessibility built in. Use ARIA only to fill genuine gaps — misused ARIA can mislead screen readers.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT primarily an accessibility feature?
questions.explanation: alt text, labels and heading order all aid assistive tech. A background gradient is purely visual styling.

modules.title: SEO with HTML
modules.summary: Title tags, meta descriptions and heading structure that help search engines understand and rank your page.
modules.outcome: You can write a strong title tag and meta description, structure headings for search, and avoid the spammy habits that get pages penalised.
modules.intro: SEO — Search Engine Optimisation — is how you help Google understand your page so the right people find it. Whole careers are built on it, but a big chunk comes down to HTML you already know, used thoughtfully. No tricks, no stuffing — just clear, honest structure.

topics.title: The title tag and meta description
topics.html:
Two elements in the <head> do the heavy lifting in search results:

  • The title tag — <title>Best Dosa in Chennai — Anna's Kitchen</title> — becomes the blue clickable headline on Google and the browser-tab text. Keep it around 50–60 characters, put the most important words first, and make every page's title unique.
  • The meta description — <meta name="description" content="…"> — is the grey summary line under the title. Around 120–155 characters. It doesn't directly change ranking, but a compelling one earns more clicks.
Write the title for a human scanning ten search results, not for a robot. "Free HTML & CSS Tutorial for Beginners — Vidaara" beats a comma-soup of keywords every time.
keyPoints: The <title> is the headline in search results and the tab text — unique per page, ~50–60 chars, key words first.
The <meta name="description"> is the summary snippet — ~120–155 chars; it drives clicks more than ranking.
Write both for humans scanning results, not for robots.

topics.title: Structure, links and honest content
topics.html:
Search engines read your page's structure to understand it — which is exactly why the HTML habits from earlier lessons are also SEO habits:

  • One <h1> that states the page's topic, with a sensible <h2>/<h3> outline beneath it.
  • Descriptive link text — "our refund policy", not "click here" — tells engines what the linked page is about.
  • Meaningful alt text — images get indexed too, and alt text is how.
  • Semantic landmarks (<main>, <article>) help engines find the real content.
Don't try to trick Google. Keyword stuffing, hidden text, and repeating your keyword 50 times all get pages penalised, not promoted. Modern search rewards genuinely useful, well-structured content. The honest path is also the winning one.
There's more to technical SEO — sitemaps, structured data (JSON-LD), Open Graph — and the next lesson covers meta and social tags. But clean HTML is the foundation everything else sits on.
keyPoints: A single clear <h1> plus a logical heading outline tells engines what the page is about.
Descriptive link text and meaningful alt text both feed SEO.
Never keyword-stuff or hide text — it gets pages penalised; useful, structured content wins.

practical.title: Practical: optimise a page's head and headings
practical.intro: For an imaginary page about a tea shop, write:
steps: A unique <title> of about 50–60 characters with the key words first.
A <meta name="description"> of about 120–155 characters that would tempt a click.
A single <h1> and two <h2> sections beneath it.
One link with descriptive text (not 'click here').

questions.text: Where does the <title> tag's text appear?
options: As the clickable headline in search results and the browser tab
At the bottom of the page
questions.explanation: The title tag is the blue headline on Google and the browser-tab label — one of the most important SEO elements.

questions.text: What is a good length for a meta description?
questions.explanation: Around 120–155 characters fits the snippet Google shows without being cut off.

questions.text: How many <h1> elements help SEO most?
options: One clear h1 stating the topic
questions.explanation: A single, clear <h1> with a logical heading outline helps search engines understand the page.

questions.text: Which link text is better for SEO?
questions.explanation: Descriptive text like "our refund policy" tells search engines what the linked page is about.

questions.text: What happens if you stuff a page with repeated keywords?
options: It can get the page penalised
questions.explanation: Keyword stuffing and hidden text are penalised by modern search engines, which reward genuinely useful, structured content.

modules.title: Meta Tags & Open Graph
modules.summary: The essential <head> meta tags, plus Open Graph and Twitter cards that control how your page looks when shared.
modules.outcome: You can add the must-have meta tags every page needs, and use Open Graph tags so links to your site look great on WhatsApp, Facebook and X.
modules.intro: The <head> is invisible to visitors but vital to machines — browsers, search engines and social platforms all read it. A few meta tags here decide whether your page renders correctly on phones and whether a shared link looks like a rich preview card or an ugly bare URL.

topics.title: The must-have meta tags
topics.html:
Three meta tags belong in essentially every page's <head>:

<meta charset="UTF-8">
<meta name="viewport"
      content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<meta name="description" content="…">
  • charset="UTF-8" — tells the browser how to read your text. Without it, accents and other languages can turn into garbled symbols. It should be the first thing in the head.
  • viewport — the single most important tag for mobile. It makes the page fit the device width instead of showing a tiny zoomed-out desktop layout. Leave it out and your responsive CSS won't work on phones.
  • description — the search snippet from the last lesson.
If you forget the viewport tag, your site will look broken and tiny on every phone — and most of your visitors are on phones. It's not optional.
keyPoints: <meta charset="UTF-8"> ensures text and accents display correctly — put it first.
<meta name="viewport"> makes the page fit mobile screens — without it, responsive CSS won't work.
<meta name="description"> supplies the search-result snippet.

topics.title: Open Graph — control your share preview
topics.html:
When someone pastes your link into WhatsApp, Facebook, LinkedIn or X, those platforms look for Open Graph (og:) meta tags to build the preview card — the image, title and description you see:

<meta property="og:title" content="Free HTML & CSS Course">
<meta property="og:description" content="Learn web design, free.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://site.com/cover.jpg">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://site.com/">

X (Twitter) adds a couple of its own: <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image"> for a big-image card. The playground below shows what these values produce — a share card:
keyPoints: Open Graph (og:) meta tags control the preview card shown when your link is shared.
Key ones: og:title, og:description, og:image, og:url.
Add twitter:card for X's preview style (e.g. summary_large_image).

practical.title: Practical: a complete, share-ready head
practical.intro: Write the <head> meta tags for a page about your project:
steps: <meta charset="UTF-8"> and the mobile viewport tag.
A <meta name="description">.
Open Graph tags: og:title, og:description, og:image, og:url.
A twitter:card tag set to summary_large_image.

questions.text: What does <meta charset="UTF-8"> do?
options: Tells the browser how to read the text so characters display correctly
questions.explanation: The charset tag defines the text encoding; without UTF-8, accents and other scripts can appear garbled.

questions.text: Which tag makes a page fit mobile screens properly?
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag makes the page match the device width — essential for responsive design to work on phones.

questions.text: What do Open Graph (og:) tags control?
options: How a link looks when shared on social media
questions.explanation: Social platforms read og: tags to build the preview card (image, title, description) shown when your link is shared.

questions.text: Which Open Graph tag sets the preview image?
questions.explanation: og:image points to the picture used in the share-preview card.

questions.text: What happens if you omit the viewport tag?
options: The page shows a tiny, zoomed-out desktop layout on phones
questions.explanation: Without the viewport tag, phones render a shrunken desktop layout and your responsive CSS won't take effect.

modules.title: Performance Basics
modules.summary: Defer, async, lazy-loading and lean markup — simple HTML choices that keep pages fast on slow networks.
modules.outcome: You can load scripts without blocking the page, lazy-load images, reserve space to prevent layout jumps, and explain why lean HTML matters for real users.
modules.intro: A fast page isn't a luxury — for someone on a budget phone and a patchy 3G connection, it's the difference between using your site and giving up. Plenty of speed comes from a few HTML habits. You've already met some; here we pull the performance ones together.

topics.title: Load scripts without blocking
topics.html:
By default, when the browser hits a <script> tag it stops building the page to download and run it. A few scripts in the <head> can leave the user staring at a blank screen. Two attributes fix this:

AttributeWhat it doesUse for
deferDownload in the background, run after the page is parsed (in order).Most scripts — the safe default.
asyncDownload in the background, run as soon as it arrives (any order).Independent scripts like analytics.
<script src="app.js" defer></script>
Rule of thumb: reach for defer almost always. The page renders immediately and your script still runs once everything's ready.
keyPoints: A plain <script> blocks page rendering while it downloads and runs.
defer runs scripts after parsing, in order — the safe default for most scripts.
async runs as soon as the script arrives, in any order — good for independent things like analytics.

topics.title: Lean images and no layout jumps
topics.html:
Images are usually the heaviest thing on a page, so the wins from the Images lesson are also your biggest performance wins:

  • loading="lazy" — off-screen images download only when the user scrolls near them. Huge on long, image-heavy pages.
  • Right-sized files — never send a 4000-pixel photo to display at 400 pixels. Resize and compress.
  • Set width and height — this reserves the correct space so the page doesn't jump as images load. That annoying shift where you go to tap something and the page lurches? This prevents it.

Lean markup, fewer requests

Every file the page loads is a round trip. Keep markup tidy, avoid loading the same library twice, and don't pull in a giant framework for one small effect. On a fast laptop you'd never notice; on a ₹6,000 phone on rural 3G, it's the whole experience.

Professionals measure this with Core Web Vitals — Google's metrics for loading speed, interactivity and visual stability (that 'no jumping' rule is one of them). The habits here move all three in the right direction.
keyPoints: loading="lazy" defers off-screen images — a big saving on image-heavy pages.
Send right-sized, compressed images; never a giant file scaled down in the browser.
Set width and height to reserve space and stop the page jumping as it loads.
Lean markup and fewer requests matter most on cheap phones and slow networks.

practical.title: Practical: tune a page for speed
practical.intro: Write or adjust markup so that:
steps: A <script> uses defer so it doesn't block rendering.
Below-the-fold images use loading="lazy".
Each <img> has width and height set.
Note one thing you could remove to cut a network request.

questions.text: What does a plain <script> tag do to page rendering?
options: Nothing — it loads in the background
It blocks the page from building while it downloads and runs
questions.explanation: A normal script pauses HTML parsing to download and execute, which can delay what the user sees.

questions.text: Which attribute is the safe default for most scripts?
questions.explanation: defer lets the page render first and runs scripts in order afterwards — the safe default.

questions.text: What does setting an image's width and height prevent?
options: The page jumping around as images load
questions.explanation: Reserving the image's space stops layout shift — the page no longer lurches as images appear.

questions.text: What does loading="lazy" do?
options: Loads off-screen images only when the user scrolls near them
Disables the image on slow networks
questions.explanation: Lazy loading defers images that aren't visible yet, saving bandwidth and speeding the initial load.

questions.text: Why does lean, fast HTML matter most for your audience?
options: It doesn't — everyone has fast internet
Many users are on budget phones and slow networks where heavy pages fail
questions.explanation: On a cheap phone over slow 3G, a heavy page can be unusable — lean markup keeps the site accessible to everyone.

modules.title: Introduction to CSS
modules.summary: What CSS is, the three ways to add it, the anatomy of a rule, and selectors — how you choose what to style.
modules.outcome: You can write a CSS rule, link a stylesheet the recommended way, and target elements with element, class and id selectors.
modules.intro: You've built structure with HTML — the bricks of the house. Now comes the paint, the colour, the layout: CSS, Cascading Style Sheets. This is where pages stop looking like a 1995 document and start looking like a real website. And because you'll see every change live in the playground, it's genuinely fun.

topics.title: The anatomy of a CSS rule
topics.html:
CSS works by picking elements and giving them style. A single rule looks like this:

  • The selector (h1) chooses which elements to style.
  • Inside the braces are declarations: a property (color) and a value (orange), separated by a colon and ended with a semicolon.

You can stack as many declarations as you like inside one rule — color, font-size, padding, and so on, each ending in a semicolon.
keyPoints: A CSS rule = selector + declarations inside braces.
A declaration is property: value; — e.g. color: orange;.
You can put many declarations in one rule, each ended with a semicolon.

topics.title: Three ways to add CSS
topics.html:
MethodHowVerdict
InlineA style attribute on one element: <p style="color:red">Avoid — hard to maintain, can't reuse.
InternalA <style> block in the <head>Fine for a single page or a quick demo.
ExternalA separate .css file linked in the headBest. One file styles your whole site.

The recommended way is an external stylesheet, linked once in the head:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
One external file means you change a colour once and every page updates. That's the "Cascading" power of CSS working for you.
keyPoints: Inline (style attribute) — avoid; can't reuse and clutters HTML.
Internal (<style> in the head) — fine for one page.
External (<link rel="stylesheet">) — best; one file styles the whole site.

topics.title: Selectors — choosing what to style
topics.html:
Selectors are how you point CSS at the right elements. The three you'll use constantly:

SelectorTargetsExample
Elementevery element of that typep { } — all paragraphs
Class (.)any element with that class.card { } — <div class="card">
id (#)the one element with that id#header { } — <div id="header">

You'll lean on class selectors most — they're reusable across many elements, exactly as you learned in the Attributes lesson. Edit the playground below and watch the .highlight class style only the elements that carry it.
keyPoints: Element selector (p) targets every element of that type.
Class selector (.name) targets any element with that class — reusable, your everyday tool.
id selector (#name) targets the single element with that id.

practical.title: Practical: style a tiny page
practical.intro: In any playground, write CSS that:
steps: Sets the color and font-family of all paragraphs with an element selector.
Creates a .box class with a background colour and some padding, and applies it to two elements.
Uses an id selector to style one unique heading.
Confirm the class styles multiple elements while the id styles only one.

questions.text: In h1 { color: orange; }, what is color?
questions.explanation: color is the property; orange is its value, and h1 is the selector.

questions.text: Which way of adding CSS is generally best for a whole site?
questions.explanation: An external .css file linked once styles every page — change it in one place and the whole site updates.

questions.text: Which selector targets every paragraph on the page?
questions.explanation: A bare element name like p selects all elements of that type.

questions.text: How do you write a class selector for class="card"?
questions.explanation: A class selector starts with a dot: .card. An id selector would use #.

questions.text: Which selector should you reach for most, because it's reusable?
questions.explanation: Classes can be applied to many elements and combined freely, making them the everyday choice for styling.

modules.title: Colors & Backgrounds
modules.summary: Set text and background colours with hex, RGB and HSL, and add gradients and background images.
modules.outcome: You can colour text and backgrounds using any of the common formats, add transparency, and apply gradients and background images.
modules.intro: Colour is the fastest way to make a page feel like yours. CSS gives you several ways to write a colour, plus backgrounds that can be solid, gradient, or an image. Let's make things colourful — and you'll see every change live.

topics.title: Ways to write a colour
topics.html:
The color property sets text colour; background-color sets the background. The colour value itself can be written several ways:

FormatExampleNotes
Namedtomato, navy~140 built-in names. Easy, limited.
Hex#FF6B00Most common. Red, green, blue in base-16.
RGBrgb(255, 107, 0)Red, green, blue from 0–255.
RGBArgba(255,107,0,0.5)Adds alpha — transparency from 0–1.
HSLhsl(25, 100%, 50%)Hue, saturation, lightness — intuitive to tweak.
They all describe the same kinds of colour — pick whichever you find easiest. Hex is the everyday default; HSL shines when you want "the same colour but lighter" — just raise the lightness percentage.
keyPoints: color sets text colour; background-color sets the background.
Write colours as named, hex (#FF6B00), rgb(), rgba() (with transparency) or hsl().
Hex is the everyday default; HSL makes 'same colour, lighter' easy via the lightness value.

topics.title: Gradients and background images
topics.html:
Backgrounds can be far more than a flat colour:

  • Gradient: background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1f1a52, #FF6B00); blends smoothly between colours — no image file needed.
  • Image: background-image: url('photo.jpg'); places a picture behind the content.

With background images you'll usually pair a few properties: background-size: cover (fill the area), background-position: center, and background-repeat: no-repeat.

Keep text readable over busy backgrounds — add a dark overlay or a solid colour behind the text. Contrast is an accessibility requirement, not just taste (remember the a11y lesson).
keyPoints: linear-gradient() blends between colours with no image file.
background-image: url(...) places a picture; pair with background-size: cover, position, no-repeat.
Keep enough contrast for readable text over images — it's an accessibility requirement.

practical.title: Practical: a colourful card
practical.intro: In any playground, build a card and:
steps: Give it a background using a hex colour.
Set its text color using rgb() or hsl().
Swap the background for a linear-gradient() of two colours.
Add a semi-transparent element using rgba() and check the text stays readable.

questions.text: Which property sets the colour of text?
questions.explanation: The color property sets text colour; background-color sets the background.

questions.text: What does the 'A' in RGBA add?
questions.explanation: The alpha channel sets transparency from 0 (invisible) to 1 (fully opaque).

questions.text: Which format makes it easiest to take a colour and just make it lighter?
questions.explanation: HSL's third value is lightness, so raising it gives the same hue but lighter — very intuitive.

questions.text: How do you create a smooth blend between two colours with no image?
questions.explanation: linear-gradient() (and radial-gradient()) blend between colours without needing an image file.

questions.text: What should you watch for when putting text over a background image?
options: Enough contrast so the text stays readable (accessibility)
questions.explanation: Text must keep enough contrast against the background to remain readable — a WCAG accessibility requirement.

modules.title: The Box Model
modules.summary: Content, padding, border and margin — the single most important idea in CSS, taught with a live visualizer.
modules.outcome: You can explain padding, border and margin, predict how they change an element's size and spacing, and set box-sizing correctly to avoid the classic layout surprise.
modules.intro: If there is one idea that separates people who fight with CSS from people who control it, this is it. Every single element on a web page — every heading, button, image and paragraph — is a rectangular box. Once you can see those boxes and the four layers that make them up, CSS layout suddenly makes sense. We will use a simple human metaphor and a visualizer you can drag, so it sticks.

topics.title: Every element is a box — think of a person
topics.html:
Imagine a person standing in a room. That person is one HTML element. The box model has four layers, working from the inside out:

LayerThe person metaphorWhat it really is
ContentThe person themselvesThe actual text or image inside the element.
PaddingTheir personal space — part of themSpace inside the box, between the content and the border. The background colour fills it.
BorderTheir clothing — the visible edgeA line drawn around the padding. It has a width, style and colour.
MarginSocial distance from other peopleSpace outside the box that pushes other elements away. It is always transparent.
The one rule that fixes most confusion: padding is inside the box and shares its background colour; margin is outside the box and is always see-through. Padding cushions the content; margin separates whole elements.

So when something looks too cramped, you usually want more padding. When two things are too close to each other, you usually want more margin. Keep the person in mind: personal space vs. social distance.
keyPoints: Every element is a rectangular box with four layers: content, padding, border, margin.
Padding = personal space, inside the box, shares the background colour.
Border = the visible edge (clothing) around the padding.
Margin = social distance, outside the box, always transparent — it pushes other elements away.

topics.title: See it move — the box model visualizer
topics.html:
Reading about padding and margin only gets you so far. Drag the sliders below and watch the box react in real time. Notice three things as you play:

  • Increasing padding makes the coloured area grow — the content gets more breathing room inside.
  • Increasing margin does not change the coloured box; it pushes the dashed "other elements" further away.
  • The live CSS at the bottom is exactly what you would write to produce the box you see.
keyPoints: Padding grows the element's coloured area from the inside.
