Margin adds transparent space outside, separating the element from its neighbours.
The CSS readout shows the exact code that produces the box on screen.

topics.title: The size surprise — box-sizing
topics.html:
Here is the gotcha that confuses almost every beginner. By default, when you set width: 200px, that 200px applies to the content only. Padding and border are then added on top. So a box like this:

.card {
  width: 200px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 5px solid;
}

…is actually 250px wide on screen: 200 (content) + 20 + 20 (padding) + 5 + 5 (border). That extra 50px is why layouts "mysteriously" overflow.

The fix everyone uses: set box-sizing: border-box. Now width means the total width including padding and border — exactly what you expected. The content shrinks to fit instead of the box growing.

Because this behaviour is so much more intuitive, professionals apply it to the whole page at the very top of their CSS:

*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

Add that one rule to any project and a whole category of layout headaches simply disappears. In the visualizer above, toggling box-sizing shows the difference live.
keyPoints: Default (content-box): width sets the content only; padding and border are added on top, making the box bigger than expected.
box-sizing: border-box makes width mean the total visible width — content shrinks to fit.
Pros apply box-sizing: border-box to everything at the top of their CSS to avoid overflow surprises.

practical.title: Practical: build a comfortable card
practical.intro: Open any playground and recreate a simple card. Aim to feel the difference between padding and margin:
steps: Make a box with a background colour and some text inside.
Add padding so the text is not touching the edges.
Add a border so you can see the edge clearly.
Add margin and notice it does not change the box — it only adds space around it.
Add box-sizing: border-box and set a fixed width; confirm padding no longer makes it overflow.

questions.text: In the box model, which layer is the transparent space OUTSIDE the box that pushes other elements away?
questions.explanation: Margin is the outside, always-transparent space. It separates an element from its neighbours — the 'social distance'.

questions.text: Which layer sits INSIDE the box, between the content and the border, and shares the background colour?
questions.explanation: Padding is the inner cushion. It shares the element's background colour — the 'personal space' that is part of the box.

questions.text: With the default box-sizing, an element has width: 200px, padding: 20px and border: 5px. How wide is it on screen?
questions.explanation: Default is content-box: 200 + 20 + 20 + 5 + 5 = 250px. Padding and border are added on top of the width.

questions.text: What does box-sizing: border-box do?
options: Makes width include padding and border (content shrinks to fit)
Adds a border to every element
questions.explanation: With border-box, the width you set is the total visible width; padding and border are included, so the content area shrinks instead of the box growing.

questions.text: Two paragraphs are sitting too close together. Which property best separates them?
questions.explanation: Margin is the space BETWEEN elements. Padding would only add space inside each paragraph, not between them.

modules.title: Text & Fonts
modules.summary: Control font family, size, weight, line-height and alignment — and add web fonts for a distinctive look.
modules.outcome: You can choose fonts with sensible fallbacks, size text in responsive units, set comfortable line spacing, and load a web font.
modules.intro: Most of a web page is text, so good typography does more for how a site feels than almost anything else. The good news: a handful of CSS properties cover the essentials, and small tweaks to size and spacing make a surprisingly big difference to readability.

topics.title: Font family and size
topics.html:
font-family sets the typeface. You give a stack — a list of fallbacks — so if the first font isn't available, the browser tries the next, ending with a generic family:

font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif;

The generic families are serif (with little feet, like Times), sans-serif (clean, like Arial), and monospace (fixed-width, like code).

Sizing text: px vs rem

  • px — a fixed pixel size (font-size: 16px). Simple and predictable.
  • rem — relative to the page's base size (1rem usually equals 16px, 1.5rem equals 24px). Preferred for body text because it respects the user's chosen browser font size — an accessibility win.
Keep body text at least 16px (1rem). Smaller text is hard to read, especially on phones, and frustrates older readers.
keyPoints: font-family takes a stack of fallbacks ending in a generic family (serif/sans-serif/monospace).
px is fixed; rem scales with the user's base size and is preferred for body text.
Keep body text at least 16px (1rem) for readability.

topics.title: Weight, spacing, alignment — and web fonts
topics.html:
A few more properties polish your text:

  • font-weight — normal, bold, or numbers 100–900.
  • line-height — space between lines. 1.5–1.6 is comfortable for body text; cramped lines are tiring to read.
  • text-align — left, center, right, justify.
  • text-decoration — e.g. underline, or none to remove link underlines.
  • letter-spacing — fine-tune the gaps between letters.

Web fonts

To use a font most computers don't have (like a Google Font), link it in your HTML head, then name it in font-family:

<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter" rel="stylesheet">

/* then in CSS */
body { font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif; }
Don't load too many web fonts — each one is a download. Two families (one for headings, one for body) is plenty for most sites, and keeps the page fast on slow connections.
keyPoints: font-weight (normal/bold or 100–900), line-height (1.5–1.6 for body), text-align and letter-spacing polish text.
Load a web font by linking it, then naming it in font-family.
Limit web fonts (two families is plenty) to keep pages fast.

practical.title: Practical: style a readable article
practical.intro: In any playground, style a short article so that:
steps: Body text is 1rem with line-height of about 1.6.
The <h1> uses a larger size and a heavier font-weight.
A .lead intro paragraph is slightly larger and a softer colour.
Try a Google web font, falling back to a generic family in the stack.

questions.text: Why does font-family usually list several fonts?
options: To show all of them at once
As fallbacks — if one isn't available the browser tries the next
questions.explanation: A font stack provides fallbacks, ending in a generic family, so text always renders sensibly.

questions.text: Which unit scales with the user's base font size and is preferred for body text?
questions.explanation: rem is relative to the root font size, so it respects the user's chosen size — an accessibility benefit.

questions.text: What is a comfortable line-height for body text?
questions.explanation: Around 1.5–1.6 gives readable spacing; very tight line-height is tiring to read.

questions.text: What is the minimum recommended size for body text?
questions.explanation: Keep body text at least 16px (1rem) so it stays readable, especially on phones.

questions.text: How do you use a Google web font?
options: Link it in the head, then name it in font-family
Install it on every visitor's computer
questions.explanation: Link the font (e.g. via a <link> in the head), then reference its name in your font-family stack.

modules.title: Display & Document Flow
modules.summary: block vs inline vs inline-block — understand how elements flow down the page like water, and how display changes it.
modules.outcome: You can predict whether an element stacks or sits in a line, switch between block, inline and inline-block, and hide elements with display:none.
modules.intro: Before you can lay out a page, you need to feel how elements naturally arrange themselves — the document flow. Here's the mental model that makes it click: think of the page as a stream of water flowing down. Some elements are big rocks that the water flows around; others are small leaves drifting along in a line. The display property decides which is which.

topics.title: Block vs inline — rocks and leaves
topics.html:
Every element has a default display:

displayIn the water…Behaviour
blocka rock — water flows around it, top to bottomStarts on a new line, takes the full width available. E.g. <div>, <p>, <h1>.
inlinea leaf — drifts along in the current, left to rightSits in the line of text, only as wide as its content; width/height are ignored. E.g. <a>, <strong>, <span>.
inline-blocka leaf you can resizeFlows in the line like inline, but you can set width, height, margins. Great for buttons in a row.
This is why setting width on a <span> seems to "do nothing" — inline elements ignore it. Switch it to inline-block (or block) and the width applies.
keyPoints: block elements start a new line and take full width (div, p, h1).
inline elements sit within a line and ignore width/height (a, span, strong).
inline-block flows inline but accepts width, height and margins.

topics.title: Changing and removing display
topics.html:
You can override an element's default with the display property — turn a list of links into a horizontal row, or a span into a block. You'll do this constantly.

Hiding elements

Two ways to hide something, with an important difference:

  • display: none — removes the element completely. It takes up no space; the flow closes up as if it were never there.
  • visibility: hidden — makes it invisible but it still occupies its space, leaving a gap.
Reach for display: none most of the time (e.g. hiding a mobile menu). Use visibility: hidden only when you specifically need to keep the empty space reserved.

Coming next: display: flex and display: grid — special display values that turn an element into a powerful layout container. They're the modern way to arrange the water entirely.
keyPoints: Set the display property to override an element's default (e.g. make links sit in a row).
display: none removes the element and its space entirely.
visibility: hidden hides it but keeps its space — leaving a gap.
display: flex and display: grid turn an element into a layout container (next lessons).

practical.title: Practical: feel the flow
practical.intro: In any playground, experiment until you can predict the result:
steps: Make two <div>s and confirm they stack (block).
Make two <span>s and confirm they sit in a line (inline).
Give a span display: inline-block and a width, and watch the width now apply.
Hide one element with display: none and note the gap closes up.

questions.text: A block element, by default…
options: Sits in a line with text
Starts on a new line and takes the full width
questions.explanation: Block elements (div, p, h1) start a new line and stretch to the full available width.

questions.text: Why does setting width on a <span> appear to do nothing?
options: Inline elements ignore width and height
questions.explanation: Inline elements ignore width/height. Switch the display to inline-block or block and the width applies.

questions.text: Which display value flows in a line but still accepts width and height?
questions.explanation: inline-block sits in the line like inline but accepts width, height and margins.

questions.text: What's the difference between display: none and visibility: hidden?
options: none removes the element and its space; hidden keeps the space
hidden deletes the element from the file
questions.explanation: display: none removes the element entirely (no space); visibility: hidden hides it but leaves its space.

questions.text: Which display values turn an element into a layout container?
questions.explanation: display: flex and display: grid make an element a powerful layout container — covered next.

modules.title: Position
modules.summary: static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky — place elements precisely and layer them with z-index.
modules.outcome: You can nudge elements with relative, place them freely with absolute, pin them with fixed or sticky, and understand how positioning contexts work.
modules.intro: Most of the time you let elements sit in the normal flow. But sometimes you need to place something exactly — a badge on a card, a menu that sticks to the top as you scroll, a button pinned to the corner. That's what the position property is for. It has five values, and they trip up a lot of people, so we'll go slowly.

topics.title: static and relative
topics.html:
• static — the default. The element sits in the normal flow; top/left have no effect. You rarely write it.
  • relative — the element stays in the flow (its original space is kept) but you can nudge it from where it would normally be using top, right, bottom, left.
.badge {
  position: relative;
  top: -8px;   /* nudge up 8px */
  left: 10px;  /* nudge right 10px */
}
A key extra power of relative: it becomes the anchor for any absolute children — which is the secret to the next part.
keyPoints: static is the default — normal flow, and top/left are ignored.
relative keeps the element's space but lets you nudge it with top/right/bottom/left.
A relative element becomes the positioning anchor for absolute children.

topics.title: absolute, fixed and sticky
topics.html:
• absolute — removed from the flow (it takes no space) and placed relative to its nearest positioned ancestor (one with relative/absolute/fixed). Perfect for a badge in the corner of a card: set the card to position: relative and the badge to position: absolute; top: 8px; right: 8px.
  • fixed — pinned to the browser window. It stays put even as you scroll — used for sticky headers, chat buttons, cookie bars.
  • sticky — a hybrid: the element scrolls normally until it reaches a set point (e.g. top: 0), then sticks there. Great for section headings that pin to the top as you read past them.

Layering with z-index

When positioned elements overlap, z-index decides what's on top — a higher number wins. It only works on positioned elements (not static ones).

The classic mistake: setting absolute on a child but forgetting to set relative on the parent. Without a positioned ancestor, the element jumps to the whole page instead of staying inside its card.
keyPoints: absolute removes the element from flow and places it relative to its nearest positioned ancestor.
fixed pins to the browser window (stays during scroll); sticky scrolls then sticks at a set point.
z-index controls stacking order on positioned elements — higher is on top.
Gotcha: give the parent position: relative or an absolute child escapes to the whole page.

topics.title: Watch position in action
topics.html: Switch the position value and drag the offsets to see how each one behaves. Watch the key difference: with static the offsets do nothing; with relative the box is nudged from its normal spot; with absolute it's lifted out of the flow and placed against the parent.
keyPoints: static ignores top/left entirely.
relative nudges the box from where it would normally sit.
absolute removes it from flow and positions it against the parent.

practical.intro: In any playground:
steps: Build a card and pin a small badge to its top-right with absolute (remember position: relative on the card).
Nudge an element a few pixels with position: relative and top/left.
Make a header position: sticky; top: 0 and scroll to see it stick.
Use z-index to put one overlapping box above another.

questions.text: Which value keeps the element in the flow but lets you nudge it with top/left?
questions.explanation: relative keeps the element's original space but offsets it by top/right/bottom/left.

questions.text: An absolute element is positioned relative to…
questions.explanation: Absolute positioning is relative to the nearest ancestor with a position other than static.

questions.text: Which value pins an element to the browser window even while scrolling?
questions.explanation: fixed attaches the element to the viewport, so it stays in place as the page scrolls.

questions.text: What does position: sticky do?
options: Glues the element to the page forever
Scrolls normally until a set point, then sticks there
questions.explanation: Sticky is a hybrid: the element scrolls with the page until it hits its offset (e.g. top:0), then stays pinned.

questions.text: Your absolutely-positioned badge jumped to the page corner instead of the card. Why?
options: The card isn't a positioned ancestor (needs position: relative)
questions.explanation: Without a positioned ancestor, an absolute element anchors to the page. Give the parent position: relative.

modules.title: Flexbox
modules.summary: The modern way to align and distribute items in one direction — taught with a live, draggable flexbox visualizer.
modules.outcome: You can turn an element into a flex container, control alignment with justify-content and align-items, change direction, and centre anything effortlessly.
modules.intro: For years, centering things and laying out rows in CSS was genuinely painful. Flexbox fixed that. It's the tool you'll reach for every single day — navigation bars, button rows, card layouts, and the age-old quest to centre a box both ways. Best of all, you can play with it below and watch it respond instantly.

topics.title: The flex container and its two axes
topics.html:
Flexbox works on a container and its direct children (the flex items). You opt in with one declaration:

.container {
  display: flex;
}

Instantly, the children line up in a row. The magic comes from two axes:

  • The main axis — the direction items flow. By default it's horizontal (a row).
  • The cross axis — perpendicular to it (vertical, for a row).

flex-direction sets the main axis: row (default), column, or the -reverse variants. Once you know which axis is which, the two alignment properties make perfect sense — which is exactly what the visualizer in the next section shows.
keyPoints: display: flex on a container lays its direct children out as flex items.
The main axis is the flow direction; the cross axis is perpendicular.
flex-direction (row/column/-reverse) sets the main axis; gap spaces items evenly.

topics.title: Aligning items — play with it live
topics.html:
Two properties do most of the work, and this is where the visualizer earns its keep. Change the dropdowns below and watch the four boxes rearrange:

  • justify-content — aligns items along the main axis (spacing them left/right in a row). Values: flex-start, center, flex-end, space-between, space-around, space-evenly.
  • align-items — aligns items along the cross axis (top/middle/bottom in a row). Values: stretch, flex-start, center, flex-end.
keyPoints: justify-content aligns items along the main axis (e.g. spacing a row left/center/right).
align-items aligns items along the cross axis (e.g. top/middle/bottom of a row).
flex-wrap: wrap lets items flow onto multiple lines instead of squashing.

topics.title: The famous trick: centre anything
topics.html:
The single most-loved thing about flexbox: centering a box both horizontally and vertically, which used to be a nightmare, is now three lines.

.container {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center;  /* centre on main axis */
  align-items: center;      /* centre on cross axis */
}
Commit those three lines to memory — display: flex plus both centers. You'll use it to centre content inside heroes, cards, buttons and modals for the rest of your career.

You can also make items grow to fill space with flex: 1 on the items (e.g. equal-width columns), but the container properties above cover the vast majority of layouts.
keyPoints: To centre both ways: display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;.
Memorise those three lines — it's the everyday centering solution.
flex: 1 on items makes them grow to share available space (e.g. equal columns).

practical.intro: In any playground:
steps: Make a display: flex row of three 'nav' items with a gap.
Use justify-content: space-between to push them to the edges.
In a separate box with a fixed height, perfectly centre some text using the three-line trick.

questions.text: How do you turn an element into a flex container?
questions.explanation: display: flex makes an element a flex container and lays its direct children out as flex items.

questions.text: Which property aligns items along the main axis?
questions.explanation: justify-content distributes items along the main axis (e.g. left/center/right/space-between in a row).

questions.text: Which property aligns items along the cross axis?
questions.explanation: align-items aligns items on the cross axis (e.g. top/middle/bottom in a row).

questions.text: What three declarations centre a box both horizontally and vertically?
questions.explanation: display:flex with both justify-content:center and align-items:center centres children on both axes.

questions.text: What does flex-direction: column do?
options: Makes the main axis vertical, so items stack
questions.explanation: It switches the main axis to vertical, so flex items stack top-to-bottom (and the axes swap).

modules.title: CSS Grid
modules.summary: Build full two-dimensional layouts with rows and columns — the most powerful layout tool in CSS.
modules.outcome: You can create a grid with columns and gaps, use fr units and repeat(), and build a responsive grid that reflows on its own.
modules.intro: Flexbox arranges things in one direction — a row or a column. CSS Grid works in two directions at once: rows and columns together. It's how you build real page layouts — galleries, dashboards, card grids — with remarkably little code. Flexbox and Grid are partners, not rivals: reach for Grid when you're laying out in two dimensions.

topics.title: Columns, gaps and the fr unit
topics.html:
Turn an element into a grid, then describe its columns with grid-template-columns:

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;  /* three equal columns */
  gap: 12px;
}

The star here is the fr unit — a "fraction" of the free space. 1fr 1fr 1fr means three equal columns; 2fr 1fr means the first column is twice as wide as the second. No percentages, no maths.

And repeat() saves typing: grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) is the same as 1fr 1fr 1fr. The gap property adds even gutters between every cell.
keyPoints: display: grid + grid-template-columns defines the columns.
The fr unit splits free space into fractions — 1fr 1fr = two equal columns.
repeat(3, 1fr) is shorthand; gap adds even gutters between cells.

topics.title: Spanning cells and responsive grids
topics.html:
An item can span several columns with grid-column:

.feature {
  grid-column: span 2;  /* take up two columns */
}

A grid that responds on its own

Here's a small piece of magic. This one line builds a grid that automatically fits as many columns as will comfortably fit, then wraps — no media queries needed:

grid-template-columns:
  repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr));

It reads: "make as many columns as fit, each at least 200px wide, sharing space equally." On a wide screen you get four columns; on a phone, one — automatically. It's a favourite for card galleries.

Grid for the overall page skeleton and big layouts; Flexbox for aligning items within a component. Used together they cover virtually every layout you'll ever need.
keyPoints: grid-column: span 2 makes an item stretch across multiple columns.
repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) builds a responsive grid with no media queries.
Use Grid for 2-D page layouts and Flexbox for aligning within components — together they cover everything.

topics.title: Play with the grid — live
topics.html: Drag the sliders below to change the number of columns, the item count and the gap, and watch the grid rebuild instantly. Notice how items flow into the columns and wrap onto new rows on their own.
keyPoints: More columns means items share the row; extra items wrap to new rows automatically.
gap adds even spacing between every cell.
The CSS readout is exactly what produces the grid you see.

practical.intro: In any playground:
steps: Make a grid of six boxes with repeat(3, 1fr) and a gap.
Make one box span two columns with grid-column: span 2.
Switch the columns to repeat(auto-fit, minmax(150px, 1fr)).
Narrow the preview and confirm the grid reflows on its own.

questions.text: How does Grid differ from Flexbox?
options: Grid lays out in two dimensions (rows and columns); Flexbox in one
Flexbox is for two dimensions, Grid for one
questions.explanation: Grid handles rows and columns together (2-D); Flexbox arranges items along a single direction (1-D).

questions.text: What does the fr unit represent?
options: A fraction of the available free space
questions.explanation: fr distributes leftover space in fractions — 1fr 1fr makes two equal columns.

questions.text: What is repeat(3, 1fr) equivalent to?
questions.explanation: repeat(3, 1fr) is shorthand for three equal 1fr columns.

questions.text: How do you make a grid item span two columns?
questions.explanation: grid-column: span 2 makes the item stretch across two columns.

questions.text: What does repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) achieve?
options: A responsive grid that fits as many 200px+ columns as it can, with no media queries
questions.explanation: It auto-fits as many columns of at least 200px as will fit and wraps the rest — responsive without media queries.

modules.title: Custom Properties (Variables)
modules.summary: Reusable values for colours, spacing and more — the foundation of theming and consistent design.
modules.outcome: You can define CSS custom properties, reuse them with var(), set global values on :root, and see why they make theming and dark mode easy.
modules.intro: Imagine your brand orange appears in 40 places across your stylesheet, and the boss asks for a slightly different orange. Find-and-replace 40 times? No. With CSS custom properties — often just called variables — you define that colour once and reuse it everywhere. Change it in one place, and all 40 update. This is how real design systems stay consistent.

topics.title: Defining and using a variable
topics.html:
A custom property is a name starting with two dashes (--), holding any value. You read it back with the var() function:

:root {
  --brand: #FF6B00;
  --space: 16px;
}

.button {
  background: var(--brand);
  padding: var(--space);
}

The :root selector is the whole document, so anything defined there is global — available everywhere. That's the usual home for your colours, spacing scale and fonts.

Custom properties also cascade and inherit: define one on a particular element and it applies to that element and its children — handy for theming just one section.
keyPoints: Define a variable with a --name and read it with var(--name).
Put global values (colours, spacing, fonts) on the :root selector.
Custom properties inherit, so you can theme a single section by redefining them on its container.

topics.title: Theming, fallbacks and dark mode
topics.html:
Because a variable can be redefined, you can flip an entire theme by changing a handful of values. A common pattern for dark mode:

:root {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --text: #111111;
}
.dark {
  --bg: #111111;
  --text: #f5f5f5;
}
body {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
}

Add the dark class to the page and every element using var(--bg) / var(--text) switches instantly. No rewriting rules — just new values.

Fallbacks

var() takes an optional fallback for when the variable isn't set: color: var(--accent, #FF6B00) uses the orange if --accent is undefined.

This is the bridge to design systems (an Expert-level topic): a small set of named "design tokens" — colours, spacing, radii — that keep an entire product visually consistent.
keyPoints: Redefine variables (e.g. on a .dark class) to flip an entire theme at once.
var(--name, fallback) supplies a default when the variable isn't set.
A small set of named variables ('design tokens') keeps a whole product consistent.

practical.intro: In any playground:
steps: Define --brand, --bg and --radius on :root.
Build a card that uses all three via var().
Change --brand once and confirm everything using it updates.
Add a var(--accent, #FF6B00) with a fallback and check it falls back when unset.

questions.text: How do you define a CSS custom property?
questions.explanation: CSS custom properties start with two dashes, e.g. --brand: #FF6B00;.

questions.text: How do you use a variable's value?
questions.explanation: Read a custom property with the var() function: color: var(--brand);.

questions.text: Where do you define global variables available everywhere?
questions.explanation: :root represents the whole document, so variables defined there are global.

questions.text: What is the main benefit of using variables for your brand colour?
options: Change it in one place and everywhere using it updates
It only works in dark mode
questions.explanation: Defining a value once and reusing it means a single change updates every use — consistency and easy maintenance.

questions.text: What does var(--accent, #FF6B00) do if --accent is not defined?
questions.explanation: The second argument to var() is a fallback used when the variable isn't set.

modules.title: Transitions
modules.summary: Smooth, tasteful motion on hover and state changes — make your interface feel alive without a single line of JavaScript.
modules.outcome: You can animate a property change smoothly with transition, choose a duration and easing, and know which properties to animate for smooth performance.
modules.intro: Without transitions, changes on a web page are instant and jarring — a button just snaps to a new colour. A transition smooths that change over time, and it's the difference between an interface that feels cheap and one that feels polished. The best part: it's pure CSS, triggered by something as simple as hovering.

topics.title: The transition property
topics.html:
A transition says: "when this property changes, animate it over this much time." You put it on the element's normal state, and define the change (often) in :hover:

.btn {
  background: #FF6B00;
  transition: background 0.3s ease;
}
.btn:hover {
  background: #3C3489;
}

The shorthand is transition: <property> <duration> <timing>. Animate several at once by listing them, or use all to transition every changing property.

Keep durations short — 0.15s–0.3s feels responsive. Anything over half a second starts to feel sluggish for everyday UI like buttons and links.
keyPoints: Put transition on the normal state; trigger the change (often) in :hover.
Shorthand: transition: property duration timing; (e.g. background 0.3s ease).
Keep UI transitions short — 0.15s–0.3s feels responsive.

topics.title: Easing and what to animate
topics.html:
The timing function controls the rhythm of the motion:

  • ease — starts slow, speeds up, slows down (the pleasant default).
  • linear — constant speed (good for spinners).
  • ease-in / ease-out — accelerate / decelerate.

Animate the cheap properties

For buttery-smooth motion, prefer transitioning transform (move, scale, rotate) and opacity. The browser can animate these very efficiently. Avoid transitioning properties that change layout — like width, height, top or margin — because they force the page to re-calculate positions on every frame, which can stutter on slower phones.

Respect motion preferences. Some people get motion sickness from animation. Wrap big effects in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to tone them down — an accessibility courtesy (more on this in the Animations lesson).
keyPoints: Timing functions set the rhythm: ease (default), linear, ease-in, ease-out.
Prefer transitioning transform and opacity — they animate smoothly.
Avoid transitioning layout properties (width/height/top/margin); they can stutter.
Honour prefers-reduced-motion for users sensitive to motion.

practical.title: Practical: a polished button
practical.intro: In any playground:
steps: Make a button that smoothly changes background on hover over 0.2s.
Add a subtle transform: scale(1.05) on hover, also transitioned.
Try different timing functions (ease, linear, ease-out) and feel the difference.
Confirm you transitioned transform/background, not width or margin.

questions.text: Where should the transition property usually go?
questions.explanation: Put transition on the base state so the change animates both into and out of :hover.

questions.text: What is a good duration for an everyday UI transition?
questions.explanation: Short durations (about 0.15–0.3s) feel responsive; long ones feel sluggish for buttons and links.

questions.text: Which properties animate most smoothly?
questions.explanation: transform and opacity are cheap for the browser to animate; layout properties can stutter.

questions.text: What does the timing function ease do?
options: Starts slow, speeds up, then slows down
questions.explanation: ease accelerates then decelerates, giving natural-feeling motion — it's the default.

questions.text: Why honour prefers-reduced-motion?
options: Some users get motion sickness from animation — it's an accessibility courtesy
questions.explanation: Reduced-motion lets you tone down effects for people sensitive to motion — an accessibility consideration.

modules.title: Animations
modules.summary: Keyframes and looping motion — bring elements to life with multi-step animations, responsibly.
modules.outcome: You can define a @keyframes animation, run it with the animation property, loop or pause it, and respect users' motion preferences.
modules.intro: Transitions animate a change between two states. Animations go further — they let you script motion through many steps and loop it forever, all without JavaScript. Think loading spinners, a gently pulsing button, a fading-in section. Used with restraint, they add real life to a page.

topics.title: @keyframes and the animation property
topics.html:
You build an animation in two parts. First, define the steps with @keyframes, giving the name and what changes at each point (from/to, or percentages):

@keyframes pulse {
  0%   { transform: scale(1); }
  50%  { transform: scale(1.15); }
  100% { transform: scale(1); }
}

Then apply it with the animation shorthand — name, duration, timing, and how many times (or infinite):

.heart {
  animation: pulse 1.2s ease-in-out infinite;
}
keyPoints: Define motion steps with @keyframes name { ... } using from/to or percentages.
Run it with animation: name duration timing iteration; (use infinite to loop).
Animations can run many steps and loop — unlike a transition's single state change.

topics.title: Control, restraint and accessibility
topics.html:
A few more controls you'll use:

  • animation-delay — wait before starting.
  • animation-direction: alternate — play forwards then backwards (great for pulses).
  • animation-fill-mode: forwards — keep the final frame after it ends.
  • animation-play-state: paused — pause it (e.g. on hover).
Restraint is the skill. A page where everything moves is exhausting and looks amateur. Animate to guide attention — a spinner that says "loading", a gentle nudge on a call-to-action — not for the sake of it.

Respect reduced motion

Some users get dizzy or nauseous from motion. Always provide a calmer experience for them:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * { animation: none !important; }
}
This honours a setting the user has chosen in their operating system — a real, respectful accessibility win, and exactly the kind of detail that separates a thoughtful developer from a careless one.
keyPoints: Control with animation-delay, -direction: alternate, -fill-mode: forwards, -play-state: paused.
Animate with restraint — to guide attention, not decorate everything.
Honour @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) for users sensitive to motion.

Define a pulse keyframe and apply it to a call-to-action button.

questions.text: What defines the steps of a CSS animation?
questions.explanation: @keyframes name { ... } defines the steps, using from/to or percentages.

questions.text: How do you make an animation loop forever?
questions.explanation: Set the iteration count to infinite (e.g. animation: pulse 1s ease infinite).

questions.text: What's the difference between a transition and an animation?
options: A transition animates one state change; an animation can run many steps and loop
Transitions can loop but animations can't
questions.explanation: Transitions smooth a single change between two states; @keyframes animations can script many steps and repeat.

questions.text: Which property plays an animation forwards then backwards?
questions.explanation: animation-direction: alternate reverses the animation on every other cycle.

questions.text: Why include a prefers-reduced-motion media query?
options: To reduce or remove motion for users who are sensitive to it
It is required for keyframes to work
questions.explanation: It respects a user's OS setting to reduce motion — important for people who get dizzy or nauseous from animation.

modules.title: Responsive Design
modules.summary: Media queries, mobile-first CSS and fluid layouts that look right on every screen, from a small phone to a wide monitor.
modules.outcome: You can write mobile-first CSS with media queries, use fluid units instead of fixed pixels, and build a layout that adapts to any screen size.
modules.intro: Most of your visitors are on phones — for many Vidaara learners, a phone is the only device. A responsive design is one that looks and works well at any width, from a 320px phone to a wide desktop. It's not a single feature but a mindset, and it pulls together much of what you've already learned.

topics.title: Mobile-first and media queries
topics.html:
The professional approach is mobile-first: write your base CSS for the small screen, then use media queries to add changes as the screen gets wider. A media query applies styles only when a condition is met:

/* base: mobile — one column */
.grid { display: grid; gap: 12px; }

/* tablet and up — two columns */
@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
}

/* desktop — three columns */
@media (min-width: 1024px) {
  .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }
}

Common breakpoints are around 480px, 768px and 1024px, but choose them based on where your design starts to look cramped, not by rote.

None of this works without the viewport tag from the Meta lesson: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">. Forget it and the phone shows a shrunken desktop layout regardless of your media queries.
keyPoints: Mobile-first: write base styles for small screens, then add with @media (min-width: …).
Common breakpoints ~480px / 768px / 1024px — but pick them where your design needs them.
Responsive CSS only works with the viewport meta tag in place.

topics.title: Fluid layouts — stop using fixed pixels
topics.html:
Media queries handle big jumps, but a truly responsive layout is fluid between them. The trick is to avoid fixed widths and let things flex:

  • Percentages and max-width — width: 100%; max-width: 600px; fills small screens but caps on large ones. Far better than a rigid width: 600px.
  • Flexible images — img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } (from the Images lesson) so pictures shrink to fit.
  • Flexbox and Grid — already responsive-friendly; recall repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) reflows with no media query at all.
  • clamp() — fluid sizing in one line: font-size: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 2rem) scales with the screen but never gets too small or too big.
Test at 320px — the narrowest common phone. If your page works there with no sideways scrolling, it'll work almost everywhere. Resize the playground preview to feel it.
keyPoints: Prefer width: 100%; max-width: … over fixed pixel widths.
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } keeps images fluid; Flexbox/Grid adapt naturally.
clamp(min, preferred, max) gives fluid sizing that never goes too small or large.
Test at 320px — no horizontal scrolling means it works almost everywhere.

options: Write base styles for small screens, then add changes for larger ones with media queries
questions.explanation: Mobile-first means the base CSS targets small screens and media queries layer on enhancements as width increases.

questions.text: Which media query targets tablets and wider?
questions.explanation: In a mobile-first approach you use min-width to add styles from a breakpoint upward.

questions.text: Why prefer max-width over a fixed width on a container?
options: It fills small screens but caps on large ones — fluid yet contained
questions.explanation: width: 100%; max-width: 600px adapts to small screens while capping the width on large ones.

questions.text: What does clamp(1rem, 4vw, 2rem) do for font-size?
options: Scales with the screen but never below 1rem or above 2rem
questions.explanation: clamp(min, preferred, max) fluidly scales the value while keeping it within the min and max bounds.

questions.text: What's a good narrow width to test against?
questions.explanation: 320px is the narrowest common phone width; if it works there with no horizontal scroll, it works almost everywhere.

modules.title: Architecture & BEM
modules.summary: Name and organise your CSS so it stays readable and maintainable as a project grows — using the BEM convention.
modules.outcome: You can name classes with the BEM convention, avoid over-specific selectors, and structure CSS so changes stay safe and predictable.
modules.intro: On a tiny page, any CSS works. On a real project with hundreds of rules, messy CSS becomes a nightmare: you change one thing and three others break, and nobody dares touch the file. CSS architecture is the set of habits that keep large stylesheets sane. The most popular convention is BEM, and it's refreshingly simple.

topics.title: BEM: Block, Element, Modifier
topics.html:
BEM is just a naming pattern for classes that makes their purpose obvious at a glance. Three parts:

  • Block — a standalone component: card, menu, button.
  • Element — a part inside a block, joined with two underscores: card__title, menu__item.
  • Modifier — a variation, joined with two dashes: card--featured, button--large.
.card { }            /* block */
.card__title { }     /* element inside the block */
.card__image { }     /* another element */
.card--featured { }  /* modifier: a special card */

Read a class like card__title--small and you instantly know: the title element, inside the card block, in its small variation. No guessing.
keyPoints: BEM names classes as Block, Block__Element, Block--Modifier.
__ marks a part inside a component; -- marks a variation.
The class name alone tells you what an element is and where it belongs.

topics.title: Keep specificity low and flat
topics.html:
The deeper problem BEM solves is specificity — how strongly a selector 'wins' when rules conflict. Over-specific selectors create CSS that's impossible to override later:

/* fragile — deeply nested, hard to override */
#main .content ul li a span { color: red; }

/* sane — one flat class */
.card__link { color: red; }

Guidelines that keep a stylesheet maintainable:

  • Style with classes, not ids or long descendant chains. Classes keep specificity low and even.
  • Don't nest deeply. One flat class per thing beats four-level selectors.
  • Avoid !important — it's a sign your specificity is already out of control. Fix the selector instead.
A good test: if you can restyle any component by editing a single class without fighting other rules, your architecture is healthy.
keyPoints: Specificity decides which rule wins; over-specific selectors are impossible to override.
Style with flat classes, not ids or deep descendant chains.
Avoid !important — it signals specificity has already gone wrong.

topics.title: Which selector wins? — specificity live
topics.html: When several rules set the same property on one element, the most specific one wins — regardless of the order they appear. Tick the rules below on and off and watch which colour the text takes. The four numbers show each selector's specificity as inline, id, class, element; the highest wins.
keyPoints: Specificity ranking (low to high): element < class < id < inline style.
The most specific enabled rule wins, even if another rule comes later in the file.
Keeping selectors flat (single classes) keeps specificity low and predictable.

practical.title: Practical: name a component with BEM
practical.intro: In any playground, build a small 'profile' component:
steps: A profile block.
Elements inside it: profile__avatar, profile__name, profile__bio.
A modifier profile--compact that changes its look.
Style everything with single classes — no ids, no deep nesting, no !important.

questions.text: In BEM, what does card__title represent?
options: An element (the title) inside the card block
questions.explanation: The __ marks an element inside a block — here, the title that belongs to the card.

questions.text: What does the -- in button--large indicate?
options: A modifier (a variation of the block)
questions.explanation: -- marks a modifier — a variation of the block, such as a large button.

questions.text: What is 'specificity' in CSS?
options: How strongly a selector wins when rules conflict
The number of properties in a rule
questions.explanation: Specificity determines which conflicting rule applies; over-specific selectors are hard to override.

questions.text: Which is the more maintainable selector?
questions.explanation: A single flat class keeps specificity low and is easy to override; deep chains are fragile.

questions.text: What does reaching for !important usually signal?
options: That specificity has already gone wrong and the selector should be fixed
questions.explanation: !important is a red flag — it patches a specificity problem instead of fixing the underlying selector.

modules.title: Design Systems
modules.summary: Tokens, components and consistency at scale — how professional teams keep large products looking like one thing.
modules.outcome: You can explain design tokens and reusable components, and set up a small token system with CSS variables that keeps a project consistent.
modules.intro: Look at any big product — a bank app, a Google service — and notice how every button, every spacing, every shade of blue feels part of one family. That consistency isn't luck; it comes from a design system: a shared set of rules and reusable pieces. You already have the tools to build a small one, and it's the natural endpoint of everything in this course.

topics.title: Design tokens — your single source of truth
topics.html:
Design tokens are the named, reusable values of your design — colours, spacing, font sizes, radii, shadows. You met the mechanism already: CSS custom properties. A design system simply means deciding these once and using them everywhere, never hard-coding a stray value.

:root {
  /* colour tokens */
  --color-brand: #FF6B00;
  --color-ink: #0F1B2D;
  /* spacing scale */
  --space-1: 4px;
  --space-2: 8px;
  --space-3: 16px;
  /* shape */
  --radius: 10px;
}

A spacing scale like this (4, 8, 16, 24, 32…) is a quiet superpower: when every margin and padding comes from the same scale, your whole layout feels rhythmic and intentional instead of slightly-off everywhere.
keyPoints: Design tokens are named reusable values (colours, spacing, radii) — built with CSS variables.
Decide values once on :root and reuse via var() — never hard-code stray values.
A consistent spacing scale (4/8/16/24…) makes layouts feel rhythmic and intentional.

topics.title: Reusable components and consistency
topics.html:
The second half of a design system is components: reusable, named pieces — a button, a card, an input — built once (with BEM-style classes from the last lesson) and reused everywhere. Together, tokens and components give you:

  • Consistency — every button looks and behaves the same, because it's the same button.
  • Speed — you assemble pages from ready-made parts instead of restyling from scratch.
  • Easy change — update the button component or a token once, and the whole product follows.
Big teams formalise this with tools (Figma libraries, Storybook, frameworks). But the idea is exactly what you can already do: tokens in :root, components as well-named classes. Start there and you're thinking like a professional.
Even on a solo project, a tiny design system pays off fast. Spend ten minutes defining your tokens and a handful of components first, and the rest of the build goes quicker and looks more polished.
keyPoints: Components are reusable named pieces (button, card, input) built once and reused.
Tokens + components give consistency, speed, and one-place updates.
You can build a small design system today with :root tokens and BEM-named component classes.

practical.intro: In any playground:
steps: Define tokens on :root: a brand colour, a spacing scale (at least 3 steps), and a radius.

questions.text: What are design tokens?
options: Named, reusable values like colours and spacing — your design's single source of truth
questions.explanation: Tokens are the named reusable values (colours, spacing, radii) of a design, typically stored as CSS variables.

questions.text: Which CSS feature do you use to implement design tokens?
questions.explanation: CSS custom properties (variables) are the natural home for design tokens — define once, reuse with var().

questions.text: Why is a consistent spacing scale (4/8/16/24…) useful?
options: It makes layouts feel rhythmic and intentional instead of slightly off
questions.explanation: Pulling every margin and padding from one scale gives a layout consistent, deliberate rhythm.

questions.text: What is a 'component' in a design system?
options: A reusable, named piece (like a button or card) built once and reused
questions.explanation: Components are reusable building blocks — built once with well-named classes and reused across the product.

questions.text: What is the main benefit of tokens plus components?
options: Consistency and one-place updates across the whole product
questions.explanation: Together they keep everything consistent and let you change a token or component once to update the whole product.

modules.title: CSS Performance
modules.summary: Lean CSS, critical styles and avoiding layout thrash — keep pages fast and smooth, especially on modest phones.
modules.outcome: You can keep your CSS lean, load it without blocking the page, animate efficiently, and avoid the patterns that make pages janky on slow devices.
modules.intro: You've reached the final lesson — fitting that it's about respect for your user's time and device. Beautiful CSS that makes a page slow or janky on a budget phone has failed the very people Vidaara serves. The good news: a handful of habits keep your styles fast, and most you've already glimpsed along the way.

topics.title: Lean CSS and how it loads
topics.html:
CSS is render-blocking: the browser won't show a page until it has loaded the CSS. So the size and delivery of your stylesheet directly affect how fast users see something.

  • Keep it lean. Delete dead rules; don't ship a giant framework for a handful of styles. Less CSS = faster first paint.
  • Minify for production. Stripping whitespace and comments shrinks the file the user downloads.
  • Load one stylesheet. Many small CSS files mean many round trips; combine them for production.
  • Critical CSS (advanced): inline the small amount of CSS needed for what's visible first, and load the rest after — so the top of the page paints almost instantly.
Selectors are rarely your bottleneck on modern browsers — file size and layout work matter far more. So optimise what you ship and how you animate before worrying about clever selectors.
keyPoints: CSS is render-blocking — its size and delivery affect how fast the page appears.
Keep CSS lean, minify for production, and avoid many separate files (round trips).
Critical CSS (inline the above-the-fold styles) makes the top of the page paint almost instantly.

topics.title: Avoid layout thrash; animate the cheap things
topics.html:
Smoothness is mostly about not making the browser redo expensive work. Two ideas cover most of it:

Animate transform and opacity

As you saw in Transitions, animating transform (move, scale, rotate) and opacity is cheap — the browser can do it on a separate layer without re-calculating the page. Animating width, height, top or margin forces a reflow (re-computing positions) on every frame, which stutters — this is 'layout thrash'.

Prevent layout shift

Set width and height on images and media so the page reserves their space and doesn't jump as things load. That jump (Cumulative Layout Shift) is both annoying and a measured Core Web Vital.

It all comes back to your audience. On a fast laptop you'd never notice these things; on a ₹6,000 phone over patchy 3G, lean, smooth CSS is the difference between a site people use and one they abandon. Build for them, and you build well for everyone.
keyPoints: Animate transform and opacity (cheap); avoid animating layout properties (causes reflow/jank).
Set image/media width and height to prevent layout shift as the page loads.
Performance is respect for users on modest phones and networks — build for them and you build well for all.

practical.title: Practical: audit for speed
practical.intro: Review a page (or build a quick one) and check:
steps: Any animations use transform/opacity, not width/height/top/margin.
Images have width and height set to reserve space.
There are no unused CSS rules left lying around.
Name one thing you could inline or remove to make the first paint faster.

questions.text: Why does the size of your CSS file affect how fast users see the page?
options: CSS is render-blocking — the browser waits for it before showing the page
CSS runs after the page is visible
questions.explanation: CSS is render-blocking: the browser delays the first paint until the stylesheet has loaded, so leaner CSS shows the page sooner.

questions.text: Which properties are cheap to animate smoothly?
questions.explanation: transform and opacity can be animated without reflowing the page, keeping motion smooth.

questions.text: What is 'layout thrash'?
options: Forcing the browser to re-calculate positions repeatedly, causing stutter
questions.explanation: Animating layout properties forces repeated reflows (recomputing positions) each frame, which stutters — layout thrash.

questions.text: How do you prevent the page jumping as images load?
options: Set width and height so space is reserved
questions.explanation: Setting dimensions reserves the space ahead of time, preventing cumulative layout shift.

questions.text: What is 'critical CSS'?
options: Inlining the small amount of CSS needed for the visible part so it paints almost instantly
questions.explanation: Critical CSS inlines the styles needed for above-the-fold content, letting the top of the page render immediately while the rest loads.

questions.text: Which element should wrap the one main content area of a page?
questions.explanation: <main> wraps the primary content and should appear once per page.

questions.text: An image must always include which attribute for accessibility?
questions.explanation: alt describes the image for screen readers, search engines, and when the image fails to load.

questions.text: In the box model, which layer is the transparent space OUTSIDE the element?
questions.explanation: Margin is the outer, always-transparent space that separates an element from its neighbours.

questions.text: What does box-sizing: border-box do?
options: Makes width include padding and border, so content shrinks to fit
questions.explanation: With border-box, the width you set is the total visible width; padding and border are included.

questions.text: Which three declarations centre a box both horizontally and vertically with flexbox?
questions.explanation: display:flex with both justify-content:center and align-items:center centres children on both axes.

questions.text: Which builds a responsive grid with no media queries?
questions.explanation: auto-fit with minmax fits as many columns as will fit and wraps the rest — responsive without media queries.

questions.text: How do you define and use a CSS custom property (variable)?
questions.explanation: Define with --brand (often on :root) and read it back with var(--brand).

questions.text: Which meta tag is essential for a page to display correctly on phones?
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag makes the page match the device width — without it, responsive CSS won't work on phones.

questions.text: Which properties are cheap to animate smoothly?
questions.explanation: transform and opacity animate without forcing layout recalculation, keeping motion smooth.

questions.text: Why prefer a real <button> over a <div> styled as a button?
options: It is keyboard-focusable and announced as a button for free
questions.explanation: A native button is keyboard-operable and announced correctly to assistive tech — a styled div is not.
